Existing records keep their eligibility, because DEF-belief-eligible fixes eligibility at recording, and the contract/test declarations are unchanged. (5) The report's other writes, which the rule concedes ('whatever else it reads or writes'): DEF-proof-state lists its inputs, and none of them is anything a report may write. No scenario satisfies every premise and falsifies the claim.

Beliefs: AXM-no-belief-write-path plus DEF-belief-eligible (a trial record) plus DEF-report (no record of any provenance) gives no new eligible evidence, so no belief moves. Proof states: every input DEF-proof-state names (place in the graph; the admitted version with its statement, cited premises and declared sufficiency; the trials recorded on it) is fixed. The graph is fixed by DEF-premise-graph because declarations and staged proposals are unchanged. Currency is fixed by DEF-current-trial because there are no new trials or amendments, the graph is the same, and the fingerprints are the same. The rule's paraphrase of DEF-proof-state is faithful to the new wording on the admitted version (head declaration, else staged proposal) but drops two clauses: 'with that version's statement, cited premises and declared sufficiency', and the exclusivity clause 'and from nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it'. Without exclusivity, 'so no proof state changes' does not follow from the rule's own text. It does follow from the cited premise itself, so this is a flaw in the prose, not a missing premise. One reading was weighed and rejected: the exclusivity is scoped to belief.yaml and the ledger, but the positive list of inputs already fixes what the state is computed from.

To derive NOT(claim) one needs a report that alters some input of a belief or a proof state. DEF-report forbids appending any record and changing any declaration. DEF-ledger (append-only) forbids in-place rewrites. DEF-proof-state and AXM-no-belief-write-path name no input a report can otherwise touch. No derivation of the negation exists from these premises.

subject: BRN-monitor-moves-nothing
text: The derivation rule paraphrases DEF-proof-state without its exclusivity clause ('and from nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it') and without 'with that version's statement, cited premises and declared sufficiency'. The step 'so no proof state changes' leans on exclusivity, so the rule should state it. Two smaller points. (a) That clause limits its exclusion to belief.yaml and the ledger, so exhaustiveness rests on reading the positive input list as the complete list. (b) 'Changes no declaration' in DEF-report is taken to cover moving HEAD to a commit with different declarations; nothing defines 'declaration' so as to say that explicitly.

reasoning: Attacks tried. (1) Self-citation: node X cites X. X is admitted only once every premise it cites is already in the graph, and X is not there before its own admission. Nodes are identified by id and admitted at most once, so X is never admitted and adds no edge X->X. (2) Two versions of one id citing each other: a declared X that cannot be admitted, plus a staged X' that cites X. A staged proposal is not a candidate for an id declared at head, so X' is never a candidate. If X is not declared and two staged proposals share id X, the node is the id, and it is admitted at most once. A second version citing the first needs X already in the graph, and then X cannot be admitted again. So at most one version is present and no edge links two versions. (3) A declared id that can never be admitted stays out of the graph, and so does everything citing it. Being out adds nothing, since only admission adds edges. (4) An edge added later that leaves an earlier node: every edge added with m ends at m, and every premise of m was admitted before m. So every edge runs from an earlier admission to a later one. Admission order is a topological order and no cycle can form. No scenario that keeps every premise produces a cycle.

The claim follows from four clauses of DEF-premise-graph. The build starts empty and admits one node at a time. Nodes are identified by id, each admitted at most once and never removed. Admission requires every cited premise to be present already. Only admission adds a node or an edge, and the edges it adds run from the premises to the new node. Together these give an invariant: every edge points from an earlier admission to a later one, so the graph is acyclic at every step, whether the build is finished or not. The candidate-selection and termination clauses are not needed, so no unstated assumption about which version is chosen or whether the build ends is carried in. Uncited assumptions are excluded from edges by definition, and the claim is scoped to edges.

Deriving 'some build contains a cycle' would need an edge from a node to one admitted before it, or a node admitted twice. The premises rule out both: a cited premise must be present before admission, admission is at most once per id, and only admission adds edges. The premises decide the claim affirmatively, so NOT(claim) cannot be derived.

Replayed the previous attack: lemma L is declared at head citing X, where X exists nowhere, and L is also staged citing nothing. Under the new DEF-premise-graph, L's head declaration is its only candidate 'whether or not it can be admitted', so the staged version is not a candidate. X is never in the graph, so L is never admitted, and by DEF-proof-state L has no proof state and is never proven. The attack fails. Other attacks tried: (a) a staged lemma S with an undeclared id that cites nothing, and a branch B that cites S. Both are admitted, but S cites none and is not a declared axiom or definition, so B is not proven; S itself cites no premise, so it is not proven either. (b) A staged 'definition' with an undeclared id used as a root. DEF-premise-graph consistently contrasts 'declared at the head revision' with 'staged in the ledger', so a staged node is not 'declared' and cannot serve as a grounding root. (c) Self-citation and mutual citation. Admission needs every cited premise to be in the graph already, and each node is admitted at most once, so neither can be admitted. (d) Admission-order dependence. Each id now has exactly one candidate and admission is monotone, so the admitted set is the unique least fixpoint whatever the order. I found no scenario in which every premise holds and the claim fails.

The step 'no cycle, as AXM-acyclicity requires' is exactly LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity. For groundedness: a node outside the graph is never proven (DEF-proof-state). Inside the graph, the graph is finite and acyclic, and a node's only incoming edges come from its citations, so every ancestry ends at an admitted node that cites none. Proof requires each such node to be a declared axiom or definition, so an ancestry that ends anywhere else is never proven. DEF-premise-graph and DEF-proof-state now agree on the version read: the head declaration for a declared id, and the staged proposal only for an id not declared at head. This closes the earlier gap. Residual wording note, not a gap: DEF-proof-state's 'declared axiom or definition' relies on DEF-premise-graph's usage of 'declared' to mean declared at the head revision, which is the only reading the premises support.

NOT(claim) would need either a build containing a cycle, which contradicts LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity, or a proven lemma or branch with a root that is not a declared axiom or definition, which contradicts the 'exactly when' condition of DEF-proof-state. With one candidate per id, the premises no longer leave room for a second admitted version that could make the negation derivable.

Attack 1 (declaration appears): id X has only a staged proposal P, admitted. A declaration D of X is committed and P stays staged. Under DEF-premise-graph the node is its id X, and D is now its only candidate, so the node X has been restated from P's content to D's. That is the lemma's own subject, so the case is covered, not missed. If D differs, fp(X) changes, and every trial that recorded fp(P) for X is not current (DEF-current-trial requires the recorded set to equal the current one). If D cannot be admitted, X leaves the graph. X is then not 'removed' in the lemma's sense (it is still declared), but clause 1 still holds: X's own trials fail the target-in-graph condition, and dependents lose X from their current dependency set. Clause 1 says nothing about trials that recorded fp(D), so it is not contradicted. Attack 2 (declaration disappears, P still staged): P becomes the candidate. This is the same analysis, and it is a no-op when P and D have identical statement and citations. Attack 3 (restate a staged P that a declaration shadows): P is not a candidate for X, so node X's admitted version and fingerprint do not change. Reading this as 'r restated' would make clause 1 false, because trials recording fp(D) would stay current while differing from fp(P'). But DEF-premise-graph makes the node its id with the declaration as its only candidate, so a shadowed proposal is not a version of r, and the scenario does not restate r. Attack 4, on clause 3: can a candidate switch for X change the admission of some e that depends on X in neither build? It cannot. Citations are by id, other ids' candidates are unchanged, and the least-fixpoint build admits e together with its ancestor set (none of which is X) identically, with the same fingerprints. No scenario satisfying all premises breaks the claim.

Clause 1 follows from DEF-current-trial. The recorded fingerprints must be exactly the current ones, and a recorded fp(r) that differs from r's current fingerprint makes the sets unequal, whether r is still a dependency or has dropped out. Clause 2 follows from DEF-premise-graph. With neither a declaration nor a staged proposal, r has no candidate, so r is never admitted. Induction along a citation path from r shows no dependent is admitted either, because every other id keeps the same candidate and the same citations. A trial whose target is not in the graph is not current. Clause 3 also follows. The build's result is fixed by the admission and end conditions. An e with no path from r has an ancestor set that excludes r, and that set is admitted identically in both builds, so e's membership, dependencies and fingerprints are unchanged, and so is the currency of each of its trials. Pre-fingerprint trials depend only on validity and graph membership, and both are unchanged. The new precedence rule adds no unstated assumption, because it only fixes which version the single id r has. The step reads 'restated' as a change to the version that is r's candidate, and DEF-premise-graph's 'a node is identified by its id' supplies that reading.

NOT(claim) would need one of three things: a trial that recorded a stale fp(r) and is still current, which contradicts DEF-current-trial's exact-match condition; a removed r, or one of its dependents, being admitted, which contradicts the rule that a node with no candidate cannot be admitted and the rule that a node is admitted only after its cited premises; or a node that is independent of r in both builds whose currency flips, which contradicts the unchanged candidates and citations of every id other than r. None of these can be derived from the premises.

subject: LMA-blast-radius-propagation
text: The lemma never defines 'restated'. The step holds only if 'r is restated' means that the version which is r's candidate changes in content, which includes a declaration of r appearing or disappearing while a staged proposal for r exists. If restating a staged proposal that a declaration shadows counted as restating r, clause 1 would fail: trials that recorded the declaration's fingerprint would stay current while differing from the proposal's new fingerprint. DEF-premise-graph's 'a node is identified by its id; the declaration is its only candidate' excludes that reading, so I recorded no gap. The author may want the claim to say 'r's candidate is restated or changes' to make this explicit.

reasoning: Attacks tried. (1) Beliefs: can a report make existing evidence stop being belief-eligible? Eligibility depends on provenance (fixed per record), on the artifact and its hash, and on a declared test being able to measure the contract. A report appends no record and changes no declaration, and the ledger holding the artifacts is append-only by DEF-ledger. So the set of belief-eligible evidence is unchanged, and by AXM-no-belief-write-path no belief moves. A finding in a report is output, not a record, so it carries no weight. (2) Proof states: can a report change which candidate the build admits for an id? Declared ids have exactly one candidate, their declaration, and a report changes none. Undeclared ids take candidates from the staged proposals, and a report stages none. Fingerprints depend on statements and citations, and currency depends on amendments and graph membership; none of these changes. (3) Strongest attack: stage two proposals for one undeclared id X, P1 and P2. The premises allow this: DEF-premise-graph says a staged proposal is a candidate for an undeclared id and does not say there is only one. Because 'each at most once' is counted per id, a build admits only one of them, and which one depends on order. The report's own read then builds afresh and could admit P2 where an earlier read admitted P1, giving X a different proof state. I did not record this as falsified. The difference comes from any fresh read, not from producing a report, and the report changed no input. So no scenario found in which the report causes the change; the order-dependence is recorded under entailment.

counterexample: Missing premise: for an id not declared at the head revision, at most one staged proposal is a candidate (for example, restating a proposal supersedes the earlier one, or the latest one staged is the only candidate). Equivalently: the premise graph is determined by the declarations at head and the staged proposals, whatever order the build admits them in. DEF-premise-graph would need to state this for 'the graph is unchanged' to follow from 'the report changes no input'.
reasoning: The belief half follows from DEF-report, DEF-belief-eligible, DEF-ledger and AXM-no-belief-write-path. The paraphrases in the rule match the current wording: DEF-premise-graph's inputs, and DEF-proof-state's admitted version and its 'nothing else' clause, which the rule quotes minus 'its subject included'. That omission does not affect the argument. The gap is the step 'the graph is unchanged' and 'neither which version a build admits nor that version changes'. That step needs the build's result to be a function of its inputs. DEF-premise-graph gives this only when each id has at most one candidate. For declared ids it does: the declaration is the only candidate. For an id not declared at head, it allows any staged proposal as a candidate and does not rule out several; the rule itself speaks of proposals being 'restated'. With two admissible candidates for one id, 'admits each at most once' makes the admitted version depend on build order. Then two builds from identical inputs, including the one the report's own read performs, can differ. DEF-proof-state's singular 'its staged proposal' hints at uniqueness but does not state it.

Tried to derive that producing a report changes a belief or a proof state. Nothing in the premises gives a report any path to either. By DEF-report it appends no record of any provenance and changes no declaration. AXM-no-belief-write-path closes every non-evidence route to belief. DEF-proof-state excludes everything belief.yaml or the ledger says beyond the admitted version and its trials. The order-dependence found under entailment lets a rebuild differ, but it does not make that difference an effect of producing a report. So NOT(claim) is not derivable, only left open by that one gap.

Replayed the previous attack. Declared X cites P, which can never be admitted; a staged proposal also named X cites only axioms. Under the new DEF-premise-graph the declaration is X's only candidate because X is declared at head. The staged X is not a candidate, so X is left out. The build still ends, since the one left-out candidate cites P, which is not in the graph. AXM-no-silent-failure then requires X (the declared node that cannot take its place) to be reported, and the staged X is reported by the same axiom as a staged node that cannot take its place. The stuck declaration can no longer be hidden. Second attack: two staged proposals B1 and B2 share an undeclared id B, both can be admitted, and they have different statements and trials. Successive builds may admit different versions, so B's proof state can change between reads. That change is caused by version selection, not by the subject being lost, so the claim that losing the subject does not alter the proof state survives. It is recorded as a gap under entailment. Third attack: a branch whose belief.yaml subject is removed. Admission depends only on cited premises, and fingerprints depend only on statement and premises. DEF-proof-state excludes the subject, so neither the branch's place in the graph nor its current trials change. No scenario satisfying every premise made the claim fail.

counterexample: Missing premise: for each id not declared at the head revision, the ledger stages at most one live proposal (or the definition names which one is the candidate). Without it, two staged proposals Y1 (citing a premise that is never admitted) and Y2 (citing only axioms) with the same id Y let Y2 be admitted while Y1 is never reported. Y1 is not reported because the node Y, identified by its id, took its place.
reasoning: The replayed gap is closed: one candidate per declared id makes a stuck declaration unhidable, and the added 'from nothing else ... its subject included' clause carries the proof-state-stands step. The remaining unstated assumption is for undeclared ids. DEF-premise-graph says 'a staged proposal is a candidate', and DEF-proof-state says 'its staged proposal' (singular), but no cited premise says the ledger holds at most one staged proposal per id, or which one is admitted if there are several. With two staged proposals for the same undeclared id, the build admits whichever becomes admissible first. A stuck version can then be shadowed by an admitted one of the same id (the old hiding pattern, moved to the ledger), and the version that 'the build admitted' is not fixed from one read to the next. The claim's reporting clause and its proof-state clause both rely on that version being unique.

NOT(claim) would need one of four things: a node entering the graph from outside head declarations or staged proposals (DEF-premise-graph forbids any other step that adds a node), a staged proposal taking effect as a declaration (AXM-commit-is-approval forbids it), a stuck declared or staged node, or a subject-less branch, going unreported (AXM-no-silent-failure forbids it), or the subject entering the proof state (DEF-proof-state excludes it). None of these follows from the premises, so the negation cannot be derived.

Attack: id X is staged with statement B, admitted, and is the target (or an upstream premise) of trial T. (a) A declaration of X with statement A, or citing a premise not in the graph, is committed. By DEF-premise-graph the declaration becomes X's only candidate, so X's fingerprint changes or X leaves the graph, and T stops being current. (b) The reverse case: X is declared with A and a staged B also exists, then the declaration is deleted, so B becomes the candidate. In both cases X is never removed in DEF-restatement's sense, because it stays declared or staged throughout. It is 'restated' only if a node's statement is that of its current candidate. Since DEF-premise-graph now makes the id the node, that is the natural reading, and under it both cases are restatements of X, which the claim lists. A declaration with the same text as the staged proposal changes neither the fingerprint nor admissibility, so T stays current, which the claim allows. Case (c): the target leaves the graph because a premise far upstream fails admission. The target already depended on that premise in the build before the change, so the claim covers it. For a staged-only node, re-proposing it with new text is a restatement, since DEF-restatement explicitly counts 'staged in the ledger'. I could not build a scenario that satisfies every premise under a fixed reading and breaks the 'only when'.

counterexample: Missing premise: a node's statement and cited premises are those of its candidate under DEF-premise-graph (the declaration if the id is declared at head, otherwise the staged proposal). So a declaration appearing or disappearing beside a staged proposal with the same id and different text restates that node in DEF-restatement's sense.
reasoning: The step relies on a correspondence no cited premise states. DEF-restatement and DEF-current-trial both speak of 'its statement' and 'the premises it cites', but neither says which record supplies them when a declaration and a staged proposal share an id. The derivation also argues that 'the graph changes only when a node is declared, restated or removed' and that 'declaring a new node' affects no trial. Declaring an id that is already staged is not declaring a new node. Deleting a declaration while a proposal with the same id stays staged is neither a declaration nor a removal. These changes fold into 'restated' only if the node's statement and citations are those of its candidate under DEF-premise-graph's precedence. LMA-blast-radius-propagation rests on the same undefined notion of 'restated', so it cannot close the hole.

To derive NOT(claim) I would need a trial that stops being current with no amendment, restatement or removal of its target or upstream nodes. The only candidates are the precedence switches above, and those break the claim only under a per-record reading of 'its statement': the declaration's text never changed, it just vanished, and the staged text never changed either. No cited premise supplies that reading, and DEF-premise-graph's 'a node is identified by its id' weighs against it. So NOT(claim) is not derivable from the premises as worded. The unresolved reading is recorded as the entailment gap, not as symmetric derivability.

Attacks tried against the new identity rules. (1) Id collision: declared id X can't be admitted (it cites a missing premise), and a staged proposal for X cites something present. If the proposal could stand in as a second X, an edge could close back onto an existing X. It can't: a declared id's only candidate is its declaration, whether or not it can be admitted, so the proposal is never a candidate. Even if it were, a node is its id and is admitted at most once. (2) Self-citation: A cites A. A can only be admitted once A is already in the graph, but A isn't in the graph until it's admitted, so A is never admitted and no self-loop appears. (3) Candidate swap mid-build: a proposal for Y is replaced after Y is admitted, and the new version cites Z, which was admitted later. Edges are added only when a node is admitted, from the premises that node cites then, and 'never removes one' plus 'no other step adds a node or an edge' means Y never gets a Z->Y edge later. So admission order is a topological order whatever the candidates are. (4) Mutual citation A<->B: whichever is admitted first needs the other already present, so neither is admitted. No scenario that meets every premise gives a cycle.

The induction rests on four clauses of DEF-premise-graph: the build starts empty; each admission adds a node that is new, because each node is admitted at most once; every edge added in that step runs from a premise already in the graph to the new node; and no other step adds edges or removes anything. So each edge runs from an earlier-admitted node to a later one, and an edge leaving n needs a citing node admitted after n. This covers the self-loop case, because n can't be both new and already present. Nothing in the argument depends on which candidate an id has, so the restated identity rules add no hidden assumption. The claim is only about cited edges, and the definition says those are the only edges. No gap.

Deriving NOT(claim) would need some edge running from a later-admitted node to an earlier one, or a node admitted twice. The definition rules out both: edges are added only at admission, from premises already present, and each node is admitted at most once. The identity clauses (one candidate per id, content taken from the candidate) can only shrink the set of admissible nodes; they add no path to a back-edge. The premises settle the claim positively, so the negation can't be derived.

Replayed the two-proposals-one-id attack. P1 then P2 are proposed for undeclared id X, and P2 cites a missing premise. Under the restated DEF-premise-graph, X has at most one staged proposal, P2, and it is X's only candidate. P1 is no longer a staged node, so it cannot be admitted in X's place and hide P2. The node X (identified by its id) is not admitted, and AXM-no-silent-failure reports it. Variants tried: (a) P2 withdrawn. Whichever way 'most recently proposed and not withdrawn since' is read, at most one proposal is staged and the report covers that one. (b) X is declared at head and also has a staged proposal. The declaration is the only candidate 'whether or not it can be admitted', so a declaration that cannot be admitted makes node X unadmitted and reported as a declared node. The staged proposal's content cannot quietly stand in for it. (c) Build-order dependence. Admission is monotone and a build ends only when every candidate left out cites an absent premise, so every build reaches the same node set, and 'no build admits' coincides with 'cannot take its place in the premise graph'. (d) A branch loses its subject. A subject is not a citation, so it is not an edge (DEF-premise-graph), not part of a fingerprint (DEF-current-trial), and excluded from the proof-state inputs (DEF-proof-state). Place, current trials and proof state are unchanged, and the loss is reported under AXM-no-silent-failure. No scenario satisfied every premise and broke the claim.

Each clause maps to a premise. Entry into the graph comes from DEF-premise-graph (built from head declarations and ledger proposals only). 'No effect as a declaration' comes from AXM-commit-is-approval. The reporting of unadmitted declared or staged nodes, and of subject-less branches, comes from AXM-no-silent-failure. 'Keeps its proof state' comes from DEF-proof-state excluding the subject, DEF-current-trial fingerprints covering only statement and cited premises, and DEF-premise-graph making only citations edges. The one identification needed, 'no build admits' = 'cannot take its place in the premise graph', follows from the build definition: the admitted set is independent of order. The prior gap is closed because one candidate per id means the node that is reported is exactly the node that is missing.

To derive NOT(claim), the premises would have to allow (i) something outside head declarations or staged proposals entering the graph, (ii) a staged proposal taking effect as a declaration, (iii) an unadmitted declared or staged node, or a subject-less branch, going unreported, or (iv) the subject influencing the proof state. (i) contradicts DEF-premise-graph, (ii) AXM-commit-is-approval, (iii) AXM-no-silent-failure, and (iv) DEF-proof-state together with DEF-current-trial. With one candidate per id, a second proposal can no longer be the thing admitted under X, so the old route to (iii) is gone. The premises decide the claim.

subject: DEF-premise-graph
text: Wording ambiguity, not a flaw in BRN-consistency-declarations-gate: 'the one most recently proposed for it and not withdrawn since' can mean either (a) the latest proposal, and only if it has not been withdrawn, or (b) the latest proposal among those not withdrawn, so an older one comes back when the newest is withdrawn. Both readings give at most one staged proposal, so the gate claim holds under either. They differ on whether withdrawing the newest proposal brings an older one back into staging, and the author may want to fix one reading. Separately: when a declared id also has a staged proposal, that proposal's content is never a candidate. AXM-no-silent-failure only reports at node (id) granularity, so being shadowed this way is not reported as such.

reasoning: Attacks tried, all under the restated identity rules. (a) Two versions of one id: X is declared at head as a lemma citing an absent id, and a staged proposal for X cites only a declared axiom. The declaration is X's only candidate even though it cannot be admitted, so the proposal is never considered. X is not admitted, has no proof state and is not proven. (b) Self-citation or mutual citation via proposals: A's candidate cites B and B's cites A. Admission needs every cited premise already in the graph, so neither is admitted and no cycle forms. Since each node is admitted at most once and never removed, and edges come only from already-admitted premises, admission order is a topological order and a cycle is impossible. (c) A staged proposal that looks like an axiom and cites nothing, used as a root: it is admitted, but it is not a *declared* axiom or definition, so any lemma or branch depending on it fails the root condition. (d) A declared axiom that cites a staged, citation-free lemma: the axiom is not a cite-none node, so the check walks on to the staged lemma, which is not declared, and dependents are not proven. (e) A lemma or branch citing nothing: excluded by 'cites at least one premise'. (f) An ancestry ending outside the graph: a node with an unadmitted premise is itself never admitted. Also checked: the order of a build cannot change the outcome. Admission is monotone and a build ends only at closure, so the admitted set is the least fixpoint and does not depend on order. No scenario satisfies every premise and breaks the claim.

Acyclicity comes directly from LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity, and it also follows independently from DEF-premise-graph's admission rule, which meets AXM-acyclicity. 'Never proven' when ungrounded comes from DEF-proof-state's two clauses. A node no build admits has no proof state. An admitted lemma or branch needs a citation, and every citation-free node it depends on must be a declared axiom or definition. That is the ungrounded case AXM-axiomatic-grounding forbids. The two definitions agree on which version is read. DEF-premise-graph makes a declared id's declaration its only candidate, and any other id's staged proposal (the most recent, not withdrawn) its only candidate. DEF-proof-state reads exactly that version: the declaration at head, else the staged proposal. The conditions on trials only add requirements, so they cannot turn an ungrounded node into a proven one. The opening clause says the kernel builds the graph as defined. That holds by definition, because DEF-premise-graph defines the premise graph as the kernel's build. Whether the implementation matches is fidelity, carried by the cited evidence CTR-proof-dag-invariants, not by this step. Two assumptions are implicit but harmless to this claim. First, 'the declaration' assumes one declaration per id at head. Second, 'current trials' is undefined in these premises. Neither can let an ungrounded node read as proven.

NOT(claim) would need either a cycle in some build or a proven lemma or branch with a citation-free ancestor that is not a declared axiom or definition. The first contradicts both LMA-kernel-enforces-acyclicity and the only-admit-after-premises rule in DEF-premise-graph. The second contradicts DEF-proof-state's 'exactly when' condition. Because the admitted set is a unique least fixpoint, builds cannot diverge, and the proof state is a function of that single graph. So the premises cannot derive the negation.

subject: BRN-dag-integrity
text: Not load-bearing for this claim, but worth tightening. (1) DEF-premise-graph's 'the declaration' assumes one declaration per id at head; the definition never says so. (2) DEF-proof-state uses 'current trials' without defining it in the premises served: it does not say whether trials recorded against a staged proposal's statement count once the id is declared with a different statement. Neither can make an ungrounded node read as proven, because the grounding condition applies independently of the trial conditions.

reasoning: Attacks tried. (1) The several-proposals replay: undeclared id X has proposals P1 then P2, and two builds admit different versions. This now violates DEF-premise-graph. An id has at most one staged proposal, the one most recently proposed and not withdrawn since, and that proposal is its only candidate. Each id therefore has exactly one candidate, fixed by the head-revision declarations and the ledger. With one candidate per id, the admitted set is order-independent. Every admitted node's cited premises were in the graph before it, and a build may not end while a left-out candidate has all its premises in, so every build ends at the same least closed set. (2) A report changes which candidate an id has. It would have to make the id declared or undeclared at head, which needs a declaration change and is barred by DEF-report. Or it would have to change which proposal is most recent or not withdrawn, which needs a proposal or withdrawal appended to the ledger. By DEF-ledger the ledger is its records, so that is appending a record, also barred by DEF-report. (3) A report writes something outside the ledger and declarations. Proof state reads nothing but the graph, the admitted version and the trials on it (DEF-proof-state). The graph's inputs are declarations and staged proposals (DEF-premise-graph). Current-trial status reads validity after amendments, graph membership and fingerprints, and fingerprints are fixed by the candidate's statement and premises (DEF-current-trial, DEF-premise-graph). None of these changes. (4) A report makes existing evidence ineligible, for example a contract no longer measurable by a declared test. That needs a declaration change. Altering a captured artifact is excluded because the ledger, artifacts included, is append-only (DEF-ledger). (5) A report moves HEAD to a revision whose declarations match. The declarations at head are unchanged, so nothing moves. Moving HEAD to a revision whose declarations differ is a declaration change, barred. Every scenario either leaves the claim standing or breaks a premise.

Checked the paraphrases against the current wording. DEF-proof-state: the rationale's 'its declaration at the head revision, or, for an id not declared there, its staged proposal' and 'from nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it' are verbatim. It leaves out 'with that version's statement, cited premises and declared sufficiency', but those belong to the admitted version, which it argues is unchanged, so nothing depends on the omission. DEF-premise-graph: 'built from the axioms, definitions, lemmas and branches declared at the head revision and the proposals staged in the ledger' is verbatim. DEF-current-trial: the rationale shortens the fingerprint clause to 'the fingerprints it recorded'. The dropped half, whether they equal the ones the target and its dependencies have now, still follows. DEF-current-trial fixes a fingerprint by statement and cited premises, and DEF-premise-graph makes those the candidate's, which is unchanged. That step is implicit, not unstated. DEF-belief-eligible: 'a trial record, measured or imported' is faithful. The step 'appending no record, stages or restates no proposal' needs a staged proposal to be a ledger record. DEF-premise-graph says 'staged in the ledger', and DEF-ledger defines the ledger as its records, so that holds. The earlier gap, several proposals per id, is closed by DEF-premise-graph's one-candidate-per-id clause, and with it build-to-build determinism. The finding-is-not-a-record step follows from DEF-report: output appends nothing. No clause needs the implementation.

To derive NOT(claim), some input to a measured belief or a proof state would have to change while a report is produced. Every such input is the head-revision declarations, ledger records (trials, amendments, staged proposals, withdrawals) or quantities fixed by them: which candidate each id has, the admitted set, fingerprints, current-trial status. DEF-report forbids changing any of them. AXM-no-belief-write-path forbids a belief moving without belief-eligible evidence. With one candidate per id, the build's outcome is fixed, so no nondeterminism is left to argue a change from. NOT(claim) is not derivable.

Replayed the prior attack: X declared with statement A and staged with statement B, a trial of T (T depends on X) recorded X's fingerprint of A; delete the declaration. By DEF-premise-graph X's only candidate becomes the staged proposal, so X's statement is now B; X's id stays staged, so by DEF-restatement X is restated (the 'declaration disappears beside a staged proposal' case), and T depends on X in the before-build, so the claim lists this event. The reverse (declaring an already-staged id with different content) is the same case. Other attacks tried: (1) T drops out of the graph with no listed event: T leaves only if a cited premise leaves; by induction on the citation chain some ancestor is removed or restated (including restating to cite T, which forms a cycle, still a restatement of an ancestor in the before-build). The build is a least fixpoint, so it cannot differ between reads with the same records. (2) T's dependency set changes with no restatement: edges come only from cited premises of admitted nodes, so the set changes only if some ancestor's cited premises change, which is a restatement. (3) Withdrawing the latest proposal so that an earlier one, or nothing, becomes the candidate: that is either a restatement (the candidate becomes another record) or a removal. (4) Declaring a new, unstaged id: it cannot be an ancestor of an already-admitted T, since T's citations are unchanged. (5) An amendment to another trial: DEF-current-trial counts only amendments appended to this trial. (6) Fingerprints are not keyed by id, so two nodes can share one, but that can only keep a trial current, never stop it. No scenario satisfies every premise and falsifies the claim.

Sentence 1 follows from DEF-ledger being append-only. Sentence 2: DEF-current-trial makes currency a function of three things. Validity after amendments changes only by an appended amendment. The target's presence in the graph and its dependency set are fixed by candidates' citations (DEF-premise-graph). Fingerprints change only when a statement or cited premises change (DEF-current-trial, DEF-restatement). DEF-premise-graph now fixes whose statement counts (one candidate per id, declaration first), and DEF-restatement explicitly counts a switch of candidate as restating, which closes the earlier gap. LMA-blast-radius-propagation confines the effect to the node and the nodes that depend on it before or after the change. Sentence 3 is DEF-counterexample read against the present premises. One small wording ambiguity: whether an id that moves from declared-only to staged-only in one change 'stays declared or staged' as DEF-restatement requires. Read as membership in the union, it does, so I judge the step sound, not a gap.

To derive NOT(claim), the premises would have to allow either a trial being edited or removed (DEF-ledger forbids it), or a currency loss without an amendment and without the target or an ancestor being restated or removed. Every input to DEF-current-trial reduces to those events, so no such loss can be derived. They would also have to allow a DEF-counterexample that coexists with entailment, which the definition excludes. NOT(claim) is not derivable.

subject: BRN-falsification-trial-ledger
text: Wording nit, no proof weight: DEF-restatement's phrase 'while its id stays declared at the head revision or staged in the ledger' would be clearer if it said explicitly that it means membership in the union throughout the change. Then an id whose declaration is deleted while a proposal is staged in the same change is plainly restated, not ambiguously removed-then-added. Also, DEF-premise-graph's 'most recently proposed for it and not withdrawn since' leaves open whether withdrawing the latest proposal makes an earlier one the candidate again. Either reading is covered by restatement or removal, so the claim is unaffected.

reasoning: Attacks tried. (1) Sentence 1, where r's restatement makes r cite a missing premise or form a cycle, so r and everything citing it drop out of the graph: the trials of its dependents fail DEF-current-trial because their target is not in the graph. Where the target is still admitted but no longer depends on r, the recorded set holds r and the current set does not, so it is not 'exactly those'. (2) Fingerprint collision: a recorded fingerprint of r happens to equal another node's current one. This fails under the natural per-node reading of 'the fingerprints ... of its target and of each node its target then depended on'. (3) Sentence 3 with e in neither build, or with e depending on r only in some historical trial's recorded set: the trial is not current in either build, so its status is unchanged. (4) Sentence 3 re-admission: the DEF-premise-graph end condition gives induction on the first build's admission order. The earliest ancestor of e left out of the other build would have all its premises in, which contradicts the end condition. So e and its ancestors are re-admitted with identical candidates and fingerprints. (5) Removal of a declared r that still has a staged proposal: the proposal becomes r's candidate, but the claim's own clause 'neither declared nor staged' excludes this. (6) Strongest: a bundled change. One revision removes r and also restates n1 (which cited r) back to an earlier statement that does not cite r. A trial T of n2 (which cites n1) recorded {n2, n1-old} before n1 ever cited r. T was not current before the change and is current after it, although n2 depended on r before. Bundling also breaks sentence 3 trivially: restate an unrelated e alongside r. This refutes the claim only if 'when r is restated/removed' allows other ids' candidates to change in the same step. The claim's 'the change' reads as r's change alone, so I record this attack as the entailment gap, not as a falsification.

counterexample: Unstated premise: a restatement of r replaces r's candidate (its declaration at head or, if undeclared, its staged proposal) and changes no other id's candidate; a removal likewise changes only r. This could come from citing DEF-restatement, or from stating the confinement in the claim ('when r's candidate alone is restated/removed').
reasoning: Sentence 1 does not depend on what 'restated' means. For any change, a trial that recorded a fingerprint of r other than r's current one is not current by DEF-current-trial, and DEF-premise-graph now fixes r's fingerprint as its candidate's. Sentences 2 and 3 do depend on it. The path induction for removal and the re-admission argument for e both rest on the derivation's 'since only r changed': every other id keeps the same candidate, with the same statement and cited premises. The restated DEF-premise-graph makes each id's candidate a function of that id's own declaration or staged proposal. It does not define a restatement or removal of r as a change to r's declaration or proposal alone. DEF-restatement, which might, is not cited. The event also remains ambiguous. Staging a new proposal for a declared r leaves r's candidate, and so its fingerprint, unchanged. If 'restated' covered that event and 'r's new one' meant the proposal's fingerprint, sentence 1 would call current trials not current. The cited premises cannot rule that reading out.

Can NOT(claim) be derived from the cited premises? That would need a scenario forced by DEF-current-trial, DEF-premise-graph and the axiom in which a confined change to r leaves a stale-fingerprint trial current, makes a dependent of a removed r current, or changes the status of a non-dependent's trial. None exists: under the confined reading all three sentences follow, per the counterexample trial. The bundled-change scenario shows only that the claim is not derivable without the confinement premise. It does not show that the negation is derivable, so the premises do not support both the claim and its negation.

Attack: a change that alters several candidates at once. Trial T targets X, current before the change, and no node in D_before(X) or D_after(X) (or X itself) is restated or removed. (1) Newly admitted node N joins D_after(X): a path N -> ... -> X in the after build ends at X, whose citations did not change. Walk it backwards: each node on it is in D_after, so it was not restated and cites what it cited before. X was in the before graph, so by DEF-premise-graph every premise X cites was too, and so on back along the path. So N was in the before graph and in D_before. That contradicts N being new. The same walk rules out gaining a dependency through another node's restatement: that node would lie on the path and be in D_after, so it is excluded by hypothesis. (2) X leaves the graph: every node in D_before keeps its candidate content. By induction from the sources, all of D_before and X are admitted again, because the end state of a monotone build is the unique least closure, whatever the order of admission. (3) Fingerprint mismatch: a fingerprint is a function of statement and cited premises, and those are unchanged on D_before = D_after and on X. (4) Legacy trials with no fingerprints can only fail through (2). (5) A candidate swapped for a record with the same content changes no fingerprint and no edge. No scenario satisfies every premise and breaks the 'only when'. Sentences 1 and 3 follow directly from DEF-ledger (append-only) and DEF-counterexample.

The trial-by-trial clause in the rule rests only on DEF-current-trial's three conditions. The fingerprint is determined by statement and cited premises. Admission is monotone, from DEF-premise-graph. Restatement and removal are defined as a change of candidate content, or the id leaving both sources. LMA-blast-radius-propagation is no longer needed for the multi-candidate case, so its narrowing to one node r leaves no hole. The rule's step 'its target now depends on a node it did not ... needs some node its target depends on after the change to be restated' is not argued in the text. It does follow from the backward-path argument: an unrestated node on a new path cites what it cited before, and admission before the change forces its premises into the before graph. The uniqueness of the build result is implicit, but it follows from the stated admission and termination rules. 'Validity changes only by an appended amendment' follows from DEF-ledger: the recorded trial is never edited, and DEF-current-trial reads validity only after amendments. No clause needs the implementation.

NOT(claim) would need a trial that stops being current with no amendment and no restatement or removal in X or D_before(X) or D_after(X), or a recorded trial that is edited, or a DEF-counterexample that fails to show non-entailment. The first is ruled out by the argument above, the second by DEF-ledger's append-only rule, and the third by DEF-counterexample's own wording: every premise holds and the claim fails. None of these can be derived from the premises.

Attacks tried. (1) The old combined attack (remove r and restate a dependent d so it no longer cites r, bringing back an old trial of d): the new scope excludes it if restating d counts as changing d's candidate. (2) A staged proposal for a declared r: the declaration is r's only candidate, so editing or withdrawing the proposal does not restate r. Deleting the declaration so the proposal with the same content takes over changes r's candidate but not r's statement or citations. That is neither a restatement nor a removal, so the change is out of scope and the lemma claims nothing. (3) Dependents that gain or lose r: a path from r runs through nodes that cite r, and their citations are fixed. So only r's own admission can change who depends on r (r restated to cite a missing premise, or to cite its own dependent and form a cycle). Every node this touches depends on r in one of the two builds, so clause 3 excludes it. (4) Clause 3 induction: if e is admitted, its whole ancestor closure is admitted and acyclic and does not contain r. The same candidates give the same closure and the same fingerprints in the other build, and a build admits every node whose ancestors are all admitted. That holds. Two scenarios do break the claim, but each needs a contested reading, so I recorded them as the entailment gap and not as a falsification. (a) One commit restates r and also edits the declaration of an unrelated e. e's candidate is still its declaration, but its content changed, so e's trials go stale and clause 3 fails. The same move rebuilds the combined attack: remove r and edit d's declaration back to an older statement that does not cite r, and an old trial of d is current again, so clause 2 fails. (b) Fingerprints collide across ids: X depends on r, s and t, with fp(r)=fp(s)=A and fp(t)=B before the change. r is restated so fp(r)=B. The recorded collection {fx,A,B} equals the current {fx,B,A}, so under a collection reading the trial stays current and clause 1 fails.

counterexample: Needed premises: (a) 'changes no other id's candidate' means that no other id's statement or cited premises change, and no id gains or loses a candidate; that is, no id other than r is restated or removed as DEF-restatement defines them. (b) DEF-current-trial matches recorded fingerprints node by node, keyed by id, and does not compare them as a collection.
reasoning: There are two unstated assumptions. (1) DEF-restatement separates a candidate whose own content changes from a candidate that becomes another record, so 'changes no other id's candidate' can be read as 'no other id's candidate becomes another record'. That reading still allows an edit to another declaration's text. The derivation's step 'the other build gives e ... the same candidate, ... the same fingerprints' needs the content to be the same, not just the record. (2) The derivation paraphrases DEF-current-trial as comparing 'the one it recorded for r' with 'r's fingerprint now', which is a node-by-node match by id. But DEF-current-trial says only that the recorded fingerprints 'are exactly those' the nodes have now, and it makes a fingerprint depend on statement and citations alone, without the id. So two distinct nodes can share a fingerprint, and a comparison of collections can pass after r is restated. The other paraphrases are faithful: removal leaves no candidate, admission needs every cited premise, a restatement changes the fingerprint, and a node outside the graph means the trial is not current.

Under readings the premises allow, NOT(claim) can be derived. If a candidate may keep its record while its content changes, a commit that restates r and edits an independent e's declaration makes e's trials stop being current, which contradicts clause 3. Under the collection reading of 'exactly those', the r/s/t fingerprint collision keeps a trial current even though it recorded r's old fingerprint, which contradicts clause 1. Under the id-keyed, content-fixed readings the claim holds. So the premises as worded do not decide it.

I tried to build a scenario where every premise holds, the subject of branch B is removed from belief.yaml by a commit, and B's proof state still changes. For that to happen, the subject would have to reach one of the four inputs DEF-proof-state allows. (a) Place in the graph: under DEF-premise-graph, a node is admitted only because of the premises it cites, and only a citation is an edge. The subject is not cited, so B's admission and its dependencies are unchanged. (b) Admitted version and declared sufficiency: removing the subject from belief.yaml is a change to belief.yaml, not to B's declaration or staged proposal. The only candidate for B's id is unchanged, and so are its statement, premises and sufficiency. (c) Which trials are current, attacked through the id-for-id rule: the recorded ids are B and the nodes B depended on. Losing the subject adds or removes no citation, so the set of ids is the same now. Each fingerprint is determined by statement and cited premises, so it is a function of those two alone, and neither changed, so every fingerprint matches id for id. A trial without fingerprints is current whatever the subject is. Validity changes only through appended amendments, and losing a subject is not an amendment. B stays in the graph. (d) Anything else: DEF-proof-state excludes the subject by name. I then replayed the attacks on unadmitted nodes that are never reported. First, a staged proposal hidden behind a declaration of the same id: it is not a node, because a node is its id and the declaration is that id's only candidate. So the claim does not require it to be reported. Second, a node whose declaration cannot be admitted, or a node in a citation cycle: none is ever admitted. AXM-no-silent-failure requires such a node to be reported, and because builds only add nodes and stop at closure, 'no build admits it' coincides with 'cannot take its place'. Third, a branch that loses its subject and is also unadmitted: it had no proof state, it keeps none, and AXM-no-silent-failure still requires it to be reported. None of these scenarios breaks the claim.

I checked each clause against a premise. The graph contents come from DEF-premise-graph. That a staged proposal is not a declaration comes from AXM-commit-is-approval. Reporting comes from AXM-no-silent-failure, where 'no build admits' is read as 'cannot take its place'; the two coincide because the build is monotone and closes, so every build admits the same set. That the proof state is kept comes from DEF-proof-state, which names the subject as excluded, together with DEF-current-trial, where each fingerprint is determined by statement and premises alone, so the id-for-id comparison sees no change. I looked for an assumed link from the subject to the statement, the ids, the validity of trials or the declared sufficiency, and found none. The premises treat the subject as separate data outside all of these.

To derive 'losing the subject changes the proof state', the subject would have to reach one of these: admission, the edges, the admitted version, a fingerprint's inputs, the set of dependency ids, or the validity of a trial. It reaches none of them. A fingerprint is a function of statement and premises, and DEF-proof-state excludes the subject by name. Deriving 'an unadmitted declared or staged node goes unreported' would contradict AXM-no-silent-failure. The negation cannot be derived.

Attack 1 (id-for-id fingerprints): I looked for a report that makes a trial's recorded fingerprints stop matching, or start matching, the ones its target and dependencies have now. Under DEF-current-trial that needs one of three things: the set of ids the target now depends on changes, some node's statement or cited premises change, or the recorded fingerprints change. The recorded fingerprints sit in an append-only ledger (DEF-ledger), and a report appends nothing (DEF-report). A node's fingerprint is determined only by its statement and cited premises, and by DEF-premise-graph those belong to the node's candidate: its declaration at head, or its staged proposal. A report changes no declaration and appends no record, so it neither stages nor withdraws a proposal. So every candidate, statement, citation, edge and dependency set stays the same, and the id-for-id comparison gives the same answer. Attack 2: a report that moves the repository head but leaves every declaration unchanged. The premise graph reads only the declarations at head, so nothing changes. Attack 3: build order. With one candidate per id and admission requiring every cited premise already in the graph, the finished build is the unique set of nodes whose citations are all grounded, so the same inputs give the same graph. Attack 4 (validity): validity after amendments depends on amendments, and a report appends none. None of these produces a scenario where every premise holds and some belief or proof state moves.

Checked the rationale's paraphrase against the exact new wording. The paraphrase says currency 'depends on its validity after amendments, its target being in the premise graph, and the fingerprints it recorded'. That is incomplete. It leaves out the other side of the comparison, the fingerprints the target and the nodes it now depends on have now, compared id for id with the same ids and the same fingerprint per id. It also leaves out the case of a trial that recorded no fingerprints. The step still goes through from cited premises alone. 'Leaves the graph unchanged' together with DEF-premise-graph fixes the dependency set and each node's candidate, so it fixes each node's statement and citations. DEF-current-trial ('determined by its statement and the premises it cites') then fixes each current fingerprint. So the omission is loose wording, not an unstated assumption. The belief half needs belief-eligible evidence to be a ledger record, and DEF-belief-eligible (a trial record) with DEF-ledger (trials, for both servers) supplies that. The staging half needs a staged proposal to be ledger content, and DEF-premise-graph's 'proposals staged in the ledger' supplies that, with append-only and 'appends no record' covering any record type. The derivation should name the current-fingerprint side explicitly, but no premise is missing.

I tried to derive NOT(claim), that some report changes a measured belief or a proof state. By AXM-no-belief-write-path a belief moves only through belief-eligible evidence, which is a ledger trial record. By DEF-proof-state a proof state is computed only from the graph, the admitted version, declared sufficiency and the trials recorded on the node, with currency governed by DEF-current-trial. All of these inputs are functions of the declarations and the ledger, and by DEF-report a report changes neither. No premise lets a reader's output feed any of these inputs, so the negation cannot be derived.

subject: BRN-monitor-moves-nothing
text: The derivation paraphrases DEF-current-trial as depending on 'validity after amendments, its target being in the premise graph, and the fingerprints it recorded'. That misses the other side of the new id-for-id comparison: the fingerprints the target and the nodes it NOW depends on have now, compared id for id. It also misses the case of a trial that recorded no fingerprints. The conclusion still follows because 'graph unchanged' fixes those. The author might restate the rationale so it says: a report leaves each node's candidate, and so its statement, citations and dependency set, unchanged, so every current fingerprint and every id set compared is unchanged.

reasoning: Attacks tried, each from the premises only, assuming a trial of T that was current just before a change. (1) Multi-id change: declare P (new id) and restate unrelated U together. By DEF-premise-graph the build is order-independent (the first node of one maximal build missing from another would have all premises present, violating the end condition), so every old ancestor of T keeps an unchanged candidate unless restated/removed, and by induction is re-admitted with the same citations; T stays in the graph with the same ancestor set and, since a fingerprint is determined by statement and cited premises, the same fingerprints id for id. The trial stays current. (2) Newly declared id admitting a node: for T to gain it as an ancestor, some node on the new path to T must cite it; walking back from T through unchanged nodes stays inside the old ancestor set, so the first node that cites outside it had its cited premises change and is restated under DEF-restatement -- an ancestor in the before-build. (3) Recorded id set differs from current one: lost ids require an old ancestor restated (citations changed) or removed; gained ids reduce to (2). (4) Target leaving the graph with no ancestor touched: impossible by the re-admission induction in (1). (5) Candidate swap with identical content (declaration appearing beside a staged proposal): not a restatement, fingerprints unchanged, trial stays current -- consistent with the claim. (6) Legacy trial with no fingerprints: can only stop being current by amendment or target leaving the graph, both covered. No scenario satisfies every premise while a trial stops being current outside the listed causes.

DEF-current-trial makes currency a function of (validity after appended amendments, target membership in the graph, recorded fingerprints vs. present fingerprints id for id). DEF-ledger makes the trial record append-only, so validity moves only by an appended amendment. DEF-premise-graph fixes the build as the unique least closure of candidates under citation (order-independence follows from the admission and end rules), so membership and ancestor sets change only through a change in some candidate's content or existence, which DEF-restatement names restating or removing. Fingerprints change only with statement or cited premises (DEF-current-trial). The multi-id case is argued directly in the derivation, not by stacking LMA-blast-radius-propagation, and each branch of it (amendment, target leaves graph, fingerprint differs, id set differs) reduces to a restatement or removal of T or an ancestor in the before or after build. The last sentence follows directly from DEF-counterexample. The first sentence follows from DEF-ledger and AXM-falsifiable-measurement. I found no clause that needs knowledge of the implementation.

NOT(claim) would require a trial that stops being current with no amendment and no restatement/removal of T or any before/after ancestor. Under the premises, an unchanged ancestor closure is re-admitted identically with identical fingerprints, so DEF-current-trial's three conditions keep holding; the negation cannot be derived. The negation of the non-edit clause contradicts DEF-ledger's append-only record, and the negation of the last sentence contradicts DEF-counterexample. The premises decide the claim.

Replayed both prior attacks. (1) Editing another id x's declaration in place alongside r: if x's statement or cited premises change while x stays declared, that is a restatement of x by DEF-restatement, which the scope now excludes; if only content outside statement and cited premises changes, x's fingerprint is unchanged because a fingerprint is determined by statement and cited premises, so no clause moves. (2) A fingerprint collision between r and another node y: DEF-current-trial now compares id for id, so a recorded fingerprint under id y is never matched against r's, and a collision across ids cannot make a stale trial current. A collision of r with its own old fingerprint is ruled out because the fingerprint 'differs whenever either differs'. New attacks. (3) A candidate switches to a record with identical content (declaration of x deleted with an identical staged proposal beside it): x keeps a candidate, is not restated, and statement, citations, admission and fingerprint are all unchanged; DEF-current-trial does not read declared-vs-staged. (4) Withdrawing a staged proposal shadowed by a declaration: the candidate is unchanged. (5) An id losing its candidate: by DEF-premise-graph that happens exactly when the id is neither declared nor staged, which is removal and excluded unless it is r. (6) Restated r that no longer admits, or that the target stops depending on: the recorded id r is missing from the current id set, so the trial is not current anyway. (7) Clause 3 for an e admitted in only one build: the admitted set is the well-founded closure, which is unique given the candidates, so it cannot differ on r-free ancestry. (8) A cyclic r: a cycle is never admitted, and the argument does not need acyclicity. None of these satisfies the premises and scope while breaking a clause. The only break I found (an amendment appended to a trial of e in the same change) depends on reading the scope narrowly, so I record it as the entailment gap and not as a falsification.

counterexample: Unstated assumption: the change appends no amendment to any trial (and clause 3 ranges only over trials that existed before the change). The scope should add something like 'no trial is recorded or amended'.
reasoning: Clauses 1 and 2 follow: id-for-id comparison plus 'differs whenever either differs' gives clause 1; no candidate for r, plus admission only after every cited premise is in the graph, applied along each path of unchanged citations, gives clause 2. Clause 3 follows on the node side, since the r-free ancestry has identical candidates in both builds, so the same admission, edges and fingerprints. But by DEF-current-trial a trial's currency also depends on 'its validity, after any amendments appended to it', and the claim's scope is spelled out after the colon only in terms of ids: no other id restated or removed, no new candidate. Nothing in the scope fixes the trial ledger. A change that restates r and also appends an amendment reclassifying a valid trial of an unrelated e as invalid (or the reverse) meets every listed condition and flips that trial's currency, which breaks clause 3. The derivation's 'each of e's trials is current exactly as it was' silently assumes validity is held fixed. The words 'and nothing else' could be read to cover this, but the colon gloss that defines them does not. A smaller point of the same kind: 'each of its trials' should be limited to trials that existed before the change, because a trial recorded during the change has no earlier currency to preserve.

I tried to derive NOT(claim) from the premises. For clauses 1 and 2 the negation would need a stale fingerprint of r to match, or a removed r (or something downstream of it) to be admitted, and DEF-current-trial and DEF-premise-graph each rule that out. For clause 3 the negation would need an r-free ancestor of e to change its candidate, admission or fingerprint, and the scope forbids every such node-level change. The one route to the negation is an amendment to a trial of e, which depends on how the claim's own scope is read, not on anything the premises leave undecided. It is recorded as the entailment gap, not here.

Attacks tried, all within the stated hypothesis (only r restated or removed, no id gains a candidate, no trial or amendment recorded). (i) r restated back to an earlier content, so an old trial's recorded fingerprint of r equals r's new one: the first clause covers only trials that recorded a fingerprint 'other than r's new one', so this is outside it. (ii) r restated to cite itself or a missing premise, so r leaves the graph: a trial that recorded an old fingerprint of r fails the id-for-id match either way (r in the target's present dependencies with a different fingerprint, or r absent so the id sets differ), and dependents of r leave the graph too. (iii) r removed while a dependent t's candidate swaps to another record with identical content: by DEF-restatement that is not a restatement, so t's citations are unchanged, and induction along the path from r keeps t out of the graph. (iv) e depends on r in neither build but holds an old trial that recorded r's fingerprint from an earlier era: its recorded id set already differs from e's present dependencies, so it is not current before or after, and nothing changes. (v) e in the before-build but dropped from the after-build: take the node of e's citation closure that was admitted earliest in the before-build and is missing after; all its cited premises are in the closure, unchanged and admitted, so it is a left-out candidate whose premises are all in the graph, which contradicts DEF-premise-graph's end condition. The converse direction uses 'no id that had no candidate gains one'. (vi) Other ids swap candidates with identical content: not restatements, fingerprints identical. (vii) Pre-fingerprint trials of dependents when r is restated: the claim says nothing about them. None of these breaks the claim.

Every step rests on a cited premise. Validity is frozen because the hypothesis excludes appended amendments, which closes the earlier amendments gap. Fingerprint inequality after a restatement follows from DEF-current-trial ('differs whenever either differs') together with DEF-restatement. Removal follows from DEF-premise-graph: no candidate means no admission, and admission requires every cited premise to be present. The derivation compresses one step, 'the other build admits e with the same nodes behind it'. It is not stated outright but follows from DEF-premise-graph alone, by the minimal-missing-node argument over admission order plus the end condition, and the same argument shows a build's node set does not depend on admission order. The derivation also correctly declines to claim AXM-blast-radius-invalidation for pre-fingerprint trials. I found no unstated assumption.

Deriving NOT(claim) would need one of three things: (a) a trial that recorded a fingerprint of r other than r's present one still being current, which contradicts DEF-current-trial's id-for-id equality; (b) a node depending on a removed r being admitted, which contradicts DEF-premise-graph's admission rule applied along the path; or (c) a node depending on r in neither build changing whether it is current, which contradicts the closure argument (same candidates, same citations, same fingerprints, same validity). None is derivable from the premises.

Attacks tried. (i) Clause 1: an out-of-band rewrite of the ledger's storage that drops or edits a trial. This violates DEF-ledger's append-only premise, so it refutes nothing. (ii) Clause 2, a trial stops being current because a new id gains a candidate: every node in the graph cites only nodes already admitted, so a newly admitted id cannot enter an existing node's dependency set; only out-of-graph nodes can be newly admitted, and that makes trials current rather than stopping them. (iii) A declaration appears beside a staged proposal with identical content: by DEF-restatement this is not a restatement, fingerprints are unchanged, and nothing changes. (iv) The target's dependency set grows with no node restated: walk back along the new path from the target. If every node on it kept its citations, the path existed in the before-build with the target admitted, so the new node was already admitted, which is a contradiction. So some node in the after-build's dependency set was restated, which the clause covers. (v) A trial recorded a node the target depends on in neither build: it was already not current (the id sets differ), so it cannot 'stop' being current. (vi) A simultaneous change to several candidates: judged trial by trial, each of DEF-current-trial's three conditions changes only through an amendment to that trial or through restatement or removal of a node in the before- or after-build dependency set, by the closure argument, without needing LMA's single-change hypothesis. (vii) Clause 3: a scenario that satisfies all present premises while the present claim fails is a model of the premises without the claim, which is non-entailment. None of these breaks the claim.

Clause 1 follows from DEF-ledger (trials are part of the append-only records). Clause 2 follows from DEF-current-trial: amendments only change validity, and the graph and the fingerprints change only through what DEF-premise-graph builds from and DEF-restatement names. The per-trial argument handles multi-candidate changes, and LMA-blast-radius-propagation covers the single-node case. Clause 3 is DEF-counterexample read against the present premises. One wording note: 'an appended amendment reclassifies it' should be read as an amendment that changes its validity, the only amendment effect DEF-current-trial counts. That is a reading, not a missing premise. No unstated assumption found.

NOT(claim) would need a trial that is edited or removed (contradicts DEF-ledger), a trial that stops being current with no amendment and no restatement or removal of its target or of a node it depends on in either build (contradicts the closure argument from DEF-premise-graph together with DEF-current-trial), or a premise-satisfying scenario where the claim fails that still leaves the claim entailed (contradicts DEF-counterexample). None is derivable from the premises.

counterexample: The human commits the goal-set declarations (commit H1). They declare tests T1 and T2 and a policy P that adopts on T1's result. An agent commit A1, whose message carries Co-Authored-By: Claude, changes a tracked file that only T2 names in reads:. So A1 changes the goal set by DEF-goal-set and is an agent commit by DEF-agent-commit. A1 is refused, made anyway, and is reported; the human has not committed the goal set since. A1 touches neither the policy declarations nor any file T1 names. An adoption under P is then recorded with no human named as approver; it rests on H1's commit of P and on T1's human-committed files. AXM-commit-is-approval holds: P took effect from the committed revision, and the verdicts are computed from committed content and the ledger. AXM-goal-set-is-human holds: A1 was refused, made anyway, is reported until the human next commits the goal set, and nothing treats A1 as the human's approval. No premise requires an approver for an adoption. So while A1 is reported, an adoption under a policy declared in the goal-set declarations went through without a human named as its approver, and clause 3 fails.
reasoning: Clauses 1 and 2 restate AXM-goal-set-is-human under DEF-agent-commit and DEF-goal-set and survive. Clause 3 (an adoption needs a named human approver while an agent commit is reported) fails in a scenario that satisfies every cited premise. No premise mentions adoption, policy or approver. Under the derivation's own reading that the human's commit of a policy is its approval, the adoption below still rests on a human approval, so the derivation's step 'rests on no approval of the human's' does not hold here.

counterexample: The claim needs a premise saying that an adoption under a policy declared in the goal set requires the human's approval of the goal set as it stands at the head revision (not just the human's earlier commit of the policy), and that while an agent commit to the goal set is reported, only a human named as the adoption's approver supplies that approval. It also needs a premise saying that a human's commit of a declaration is the human's approval of it, which AXM-commit-is-approval does not state despite its name.
reasoning: Clauses 1 and 2 are entailed. Clause 3 introduces adoption, policy and approver, which no premise defines or constrains. The derivation also reads AXM-commit-is-approval as saying 'a policy declared in goals.yaml was approved by the human's commit of it', but that axiom only says a declaration takes effect from the committed revision and that verdicts are computed from committed content and the ledger. It says nothing about approval or about whose commit it was. Even granting that reading, a later agent commit that does not touch the policy does not take away the human's earlier approval of it. AXM-goal-set-is-human only says the agent commit itself does not stand as the approval.

The premises are silent on adoption, so both clause 3 and its negation are consistent with them; they are too weak to decide it. With the bridge the derivation itself uses (the human's commit of a policy is its approval), NOT(clause 3) follows in a sub-case: when the reported agent commit leaves the policy and everything the adoption rests on untouched, the adoption rests on the human's commit and needs no named approver.

counterexample: Releases 0.5.1 and 0.5.2 both exist. At tag tdlp--v0.5.1 the plugin's manifest, its marketplace entry and the package all name 0.5.1; at tag tdlp--v0.5.2 all three name 0.5.2. So both are releases by DEF-release. A project enables the plugin as 0.5.2 published it, and its manifest names 0.5.2. The server launch specification that 0.5.2 published still installs every server from tag tdlp--v0.5.1: a version bump that missed the install pin, and no premise ties the two together. The project runs the harness exactly as a release published it, and the harness reads that project's declarations and ledger and runs its tests in its environment. AXM-pinned-and-rooted and DEF-release both hold. Every server the plugin starts installs from 0.5.1, not from the release whose version the plugin's manifest names (0.5.2), so clause 1 fails.
reasoning: Attacked clause 1 with version skew between the plugin's manifest and the release its servers install from. AXM-pinned-and-rooted says a project runs the harness as ONE release published it, an indefinite article, so several releases may exist. DEF-release fixes a release's version by agreement among the manifest, the marketplace entry and the package at that release's tag. Neither premise mentions the servers the plugin starts or ties where they install from to the version the manifest names. The scenario below satisfies the axiom whether the harness is read as the servers alone (run as 0.5.1 published them) or as the plugin plus its servers (run exactly as 0.5.2 published them, since 0.5.2 published a plugin that launches 0.5.1's servers).

counterexample: Three premises are missing. (a) Every server the plugin starts belongs to the harness and installs from the release tag of the version that the plugin's own manifest, as installed in the project, names. (b) The project that enables the plugin is the project that runs the harness it starts, so that project is the one the servers measure. (c) A declared test's environment is the project's environment layered ahead of the harness's own; no premise states this composition or its order.
reasoning: Clause 1: the derivation's step 'so every server the plugin starts installs from that tag' treats DEF-release's 'the one version the plugin's manifest names' as the version named by the manifest of the plugin as installed. DEF-release only fixes each release's version at its own tag, and the axiom only says 'one release'. Clause 2: the axiom speaks of 'a project runs the harness'; the claim speaks of 'the project that enabled it'. No premise links enabling the plugin to running the harness, for example for a plugin enabled at user scope or a session rooted in a nested repository. Clause 3: the axiom says tests run 'in that project's environment' and says nothing of the harness's own environment or of an order between the two. 'Ahead of the harness's own' adds a layering that sits uneasily with the axiom, because anything the project's environment lacks would then resolve from the harness's.

The premises are too weak to decide any of the three clauses. For clause 1, both 'servers install from the manifest's version' and 'servers install from another release' are consistent with them, as the counterexample shows. For clause 2, nothing distinguishes the enabling project from the running project. For clause 3, reading 'in that project's environment' as excluding the harness's own environment gives a test environment with no harness layer at all, which is consistent with the axiom and contrary to the claim's 'ahead of the harness's own'.
