subject: LMA-blast-radius-propagation
text: Not a defect of the lemma, which scopes this out explicitly, but a tension between its premises. Under DEF-current-trial, a trial that recorded no fingerprints stays current when a node upstream of its target is restated, as long as the target stays in the graph. AXM-blast-radius-invalidation says modifying an upstream premise invalidates ALL downstream conclusions until re-verified. Unless some other mechanism (such as a STALE mark) carries the axiom for those older trials, the axiom is not met for them. Consider a definition that names that mechanism, or one that retires trials without fingerprints.

subject: BRN-goal-guard
text: Two observations that are not counterexamples to the claim as written. (1) DEF-agent-commit identifies the agent only by a trailer it writes itself. An agent commit without the trailer is the human's by definition, so it is neither refused nor reported, and AXM-goal-set-is-human's 'only the human changes the goal set' is then not secured by this branch. (2) DEF-goal-set covers only files that a declared test names on its run line or in reads:. A file such a test reads indirectly is outside the goal set, so changing it is not 'changing the goal set'. Also: AXM-commit-is-approval's statement never mentions approval, despite its name. That is where the derivation's 'approved by the human's commit' has no ground.

subject: BRN-plugin-pinned
text: The falsification exploits the missing link between the plugin, the servers it starts, and the release the axiom speaks of. Restating the claim alone will not close it. It needs a premise (an axiom, or a definition the claim cites) that the servers a plugin starts install from the tag of the version its own manifest names, plus premises linking the enabling project to the measured project and stating the test-environment layering. If 'in that project's environment' is meant to exclude the harness's own environment, then 'ahead of the harness's own' is the wrong claim, not just an unsupported one.

reasoning: Attacks tried, each with every premise held: (1) r is restated to cite e, where e cites r. That closes a cycle, so neither is admitted afterwards and every trial of e is non-current, as (a)/(b) require. e depended on r before the change, so (c) does not apply. (2) Revert: r is restated back to content A, the content it had when a trial T of a dependent e was recorded. T recorded r's new fingerprint and is current again. (a) only covers trials that recorded a fingerprint other than the new one, so nothing fails. (3) For (c): e depends on r in neither build, but the candidate of one of e's ancestors becomes another record with the same statement and premises (a declaration appears beside an identical staged proposal). By DEF-restatement that is not a restatement, and the fingerprint depends only on statement and premises, so e's trials are unchanged. (4) e cites r, and r was unadmitted before because it cited an id with no candidate. The restatement admits r and therefore e. Then e depends on r in the after build, which puts it outside (c). (5) A legacy (pre-fingerprint) trial on e, made when e depended on r, where e now depends on r in neither build. The implied recorded set contains r and the present set does not, so the trial is non-current both before and after the change. That is unchanged, consistent with (c). (6) Order dependence: admission is monotone, and the end condition forces every admissible candidate in, so a build is the unique least fixpoint. 'The other build admits e' therefore does not depend on traversal order. None of these produced a scenario that meets every premise and breaks the claim.

(a): if the target is admitted after the change, every node on its path from r keeps its citations, so r is admitted and appears in the target's present dependency set with its new fingerprint. The id-for-id comparison then fails. If the target is not admitted, the trial is not current. (b): r has no candidate, so it is not admitted, and induction along any path from r leaves its dependents unadmitted. (c): e's citation closure excludes r and every candidate in it keeps its statement and premises. Induction over the closure, which is well-founded because one build admitted it in order, shows the other build admits the same closure with the same fingerprints. The three conditions of DEF-current-trial take the same values. The derivation compresses that induction and the uniqueness of a build, but both follow from DEF-premise-graph's admission and end conditions. Restated DEF-current-trial: a pre-fingerprint trial's recorded set is fixed as those of 'the build when it was made', a historical fact no later change alters. It therefore behaves like any recorded set, and every step goes through for it. The closing remark that this is the invalidation AXM-blast-radius-invalidation requires is commentary. Under a revert, a downstream trial becomes current again without re-verification after the modification, but the claim does not assert otherwise, so this is no gap in the claim.

NOT(a) needs a current trial whose recorded fingerprint for r differs from r's present one while its target is admitted and depends on r. The id-for-id equality excludes that. NOT(b) needs a node with no candidate to be admitted, or a dependent of an unadmitted node to be admitted, and the admission rule excludes both. NOT(c) needs a currentness flip for a node whose citation closure, candidates and fingerprints are all unchanged. Each of DEF-current-trial's three conditions is a function of those unchanged inputs. AXM-blast-radius-invalidation speaks only of downstream conclusions and says nothing that would move a node that does not depend on r. No premise yields the negation.

Looked for a trial that stops being current with no amendment and no restatement or removal of its target, or of a node it depends on in either build. (1) A new id gains a candidate. That can only admit nodes. A node citing an id with no candidate was unadmitted, so no admitted node's closure grows or shrinks. (2) A declaration appears beside a staged proposal with identical statement and premises. The candidate changes, but there is no restatement and the fingerprint is unchanged. (3) A cycle closes over the target. That needs a citation change on a node in the target's closure, which is a restatement of a node it depends on in the after build. (4) The target gains a dependency with no node it depended on before being restated. The node that newly cites something sits on the target's after-build path, which 'before or after the change' covers. (5) A legacy trial: under restated DEF-current-trial its implied fingerprints are those of the build when it was made. That is a past fact and no later change moves it. (6) Hand-editing or truncating the ledger violates DEF-ledger's append-only clause, so it does not satisfy the premises. (7) Restating DEF-current-trial itself, the change now in progress, can alter which legacy trials count as current even on nodes that do not depend on it. But that changes the premise that defines currentness. Inside the claim, currentness is judged by the present DEF-current-trial, and under it those trials changed only when their own dependencies were restated. Part 3: if the target's premises are jointly unsatisfiable, no scenario meets DEF-counterexample and the clause is vacuous, not false. No surviving scenario.

Part 1 is DEF-ledger's append-only clause, and DEF-ledger lists trials. Part 2: DEF-current-trial ('exactly when') makes currentness a function of three things: validity after appended amendments, the target's membership in the graph, and the id-for-id equality of recorded and present fingerprints. Validity moves only by an amendment. Membership and the present dependency set move only through candidates' citations (DEF-premise-graph), and fingerprints only through statement or citations. Both are restatement or removal under DEF-restatement, or an id gaining a candidate, which removes nothing from an admitted node's closure. LMA-blast-radius-propagation covers a single-node change. The derivation's trial-by-trial argument covers changes to several candidates at once: every route other than an amendment needs a restated or removed node in the target's closure in one of the two builds. Part 3 is DEF-counterexample read as a witness of non-entailment. No unstated assumption is needed. AXM-falsifiable-measurement supports only the remark that a correction is an appended amendment, which the claim does not depend on.

NOT(part 1) contradicts DEF-ledger. NOT(part 2) needs currentness to move through something other than validity, membership or fingerprint equality, but DEF-current-trial states those as the whole condition. NOT(part 3) would need a scenario that satisfies every present premise and falsifies the present claim while the claim still follows from those premises, which contradicts entailment. The premises do not support the negation.

(1) Strongest attack: X is a staged lemma that is never declared and cites declared axioms. Y is a declared branch that cites X. Both have enough sound trials, so by DEF-proof-state Y is proven with an uncommitted X carrying load. Does X 'take effect as a declaration'? The claim itself says staged proposals enter the graph. What the premises give a declaration and withhold from a staged proposal is (i) priority over a staged record for the same id (DEF-premise-graph) and (ii) the power to ground a proof as a root (DEF-proof-state requires every root to be a declared axiom or definition). X has neither, so the clause holds, though the scenario is worth the author's attention (noted separately). (2) One commit drops the subject from belief.yaml and also restates an axiom the branch rests on, so the branch goes STALE. Read literally, 'keeps its proof state' fails. In context the clause says the branch loses no proof state by losing its subject, and the concurrent restatement is a separate change, so I do not count this. (3) The subject is removed only in the working tree. By AXM-commit-is-approval that is not a removal, so no report and no state change is due, which is consistent. (4) A staged proposal shadowed by a declaration of the same id is never admitted, but the node takes its place through the declaration, so AXM-no-silent-failure does not require a report and the claim does not promise one. (5) Even if a branch's subject id were part of its fingerprint, dropping the component from belief.yaml leaves the branch's own declaration untouched, so no fingerprint moves. No surviving scenario.

Sentence 1, first half: DEF-premise-graph names the only candidates, head declarations and staged proposals. Second half: AXM-commit-is-approval gives it by contrapositive, and concretely the two declared-only effects in DEF-premise-graph and DEF-proof-state make it checkable. Sentence 2: AXM-no-silent-failure, where 'cannot take its place in the premise graph' is the same as 'no build admits'. 'Keeps its proof state': DEF-proof-state computes from the graph, the admitted version and its trials and 'from nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it, its subject included'. DEF-current-trial fingerprints only statement and citations. No unstated assumption is needed. Wording only: 'losing its subject leaves its proof state unchanged' would close off attack (2).

NOT(sentence 1) needs a node from outside head declarations and staged proposals, or a staged proposal that beats a declaration or grounds a root. DEF-premise-graph and DEF-proof-state exclude both. NOT(silent-drop clause) contradicts AXM-no-silent-failure directly. NOT(keeps proof state) needs belief.yaml's subject to enter the computation, which DEF-proof-state excludes by name. The premises do not derive the negation.

Looked for a report that moves a belief or a proof state while keeping DEF-report. (1) The report runs git commit on a human's pending edit to consistency.yaml, or checks out another revision. The head revision's declarations change, so the graph changes. But that changes a declaration in the sense DEF-premise-graph uses (what is declared at the head revision), so the output is not a report under DEF-report. (2) The report writes an artifact or a cache file. Artifacts belong to the ledger, which is append-only (DEF-ledger), so existing records and their hashes cannot be altered. A new artifact is not a trial record, so it is not belief-eligible, and proof states read only the graph and trials. (3) The report deletes or rewrites an existing record. DEF-ledger forbids that, so the premises do not hold. (4) The report edits a test file or component code. Contract state might read stale, but the measured belief, the posterior, changes only through belief-eligible evidence (AXM-no-belief-write-path), and proof states do not read the repository. (5) The report rebuilds the premise graph as it reads. DEF-premise-graph builds afresh from unchanged inputs, and the build is the unique least fixpoint, so the graph is the same. (6) Legacy trials: the build when each was made is a past fact a report cannot change. No surviving scenario.

Beliefs: AXM-no-belief-write-path plus DEF-belief-eligible say a belief moves only through a measured or imported trial record. DEF-report says producing a report appends none. Proof states: DEF-proof-state reads the graph position, the admitted version and its trials. DEF-premise-graph builds from head declarations and staged proposals, which a report changes neither of (no declaration change, no appended record, so nothing staged or withdrawn). DEF-current-trial's three conditions depend on amendments, membership and fingerprints, all unchanged. The derivation also needs no existing trial to be removed or edited, which comes from DEF-ledger's append-only clause, a cited premise. No unstated assumption.

Deriving 'some report changes a belief or a proof state' needs a write path into belief-eligible evidence, declarations, staged proposals, amendments or trials. DEF-report closes the first four for reports, DEF-ledger forbids altering existing trials, and AXM-no-belief-write-path gives no weight to a finding stated as output. No premise yields the negation.

(1) The agent commits a goals.yaml change without the Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer. By DEF-agent-commit it is the human's commit, so it is neither refused nor reported, and by AXM-goal-set-is-human it approves every policy it declares. The claim speaks of agent commits as DEF-agent-commit defines them, so it does not fail. This is a design weakness, not a counterexample. (2) An agent commit is made anyway, and a later commit without the trailer touches an unrelated goal-set file. That commit is 'the human's', so the report ends and the agent's policy counts as approved. Again consistent with the claim's own terms. (3) The agent changes a helper that a declared test imports but names neither on its run line nor in reads:. By DEF-goal-set that is outside the goal set, so no refusal is due. (4) The agent changes a data file at commit X, and a test naming it is declared only later. DEF-goal-set judges declaration before or after X only, so X did not change the goal set. (5) Approver 'a human' versus the axiom's 'the human': DEF-agent-commit implies a single human, and the claim's condition is weaker than the axiom's, so it is implied. Each scenario satisfies the premises and leaves the claim true. These are weaknesses of the definitions, not failures of the step.

The three sentences of the claim restate AXM-goal-set-is-human almost word for word: refused; reported until the human next commits the goal set; while reported, no adoption under a goals.yaml policy stands as approved unless the human is named. DEF-agent-commit and DEF-goal-set fix the terms, and the claim uses those terms exactly as the axiom does. AXM-commit-is-approval is cited only for when a policy takes effect, which the claim does not need. No unstated assumption is needed for entailment.

Two cited axioms pull against each other on the first sentence. AXM-commit-is-approval: 'Every verdict and every proof state is computed from committed content -- the declarations at the head revision and the commits that evidence names -- and from the ledger'. To refuse a commit that 'would change the goal set', a guard must judge a commit that does not yet exist: whether its message carries the trailer (DEF-agent-commit), and whether it changes a goal-set file against goals.yaml 'after the commit' (DEF-goal-set). Neither is committed content or the ledger. If the guard's refusal is a verdict in AXM-commit-is-approval's sense, the premises forbid computing it and so derive that no such commit is refused. If 'verdict' covers only the servers' verdicts and proof states, both axioms hold. The premises do not say which, so they do not decide the first sentence. To settle it, AXM-commit-is-approval needs scoping to the servers' verdicts, or the claim needs a premise that lets the guard judge a pending commit.

counterexample: Tags tdlp--v0.5.2 and tdlp--v0.5.3 are both published. At each tag the plugin's manifest, its marketplace entry and the package all name that tag's version, so both are releases under DEF-release. In 0.5.3 the version was bumped in all three places, but the manifest's server install source was left at tdlp--v0.5.2. A project enables the plugin at 0.5.3. Its manifest names 0.5.3, and every server the plugin starts installs from tdlp--v0.5.2, reads that project's declarations and ledger, and runs its declared tests in the project's environment. By DEF-release, every server installs from the tag of release 0.5.2, so the project runs release 0.5.2 as it was published. AXM-pinned-and-rooted holds in full: one release, as published, measuring that project in its environment. The claim fails: the servers install from tdlp--v0.5.2, not from the tag of the version the plugin's manifest names (tdlp--v0.5.3).
reasoning: DEF-release defines 'a release' as the code at any tag where that tag's manifest, marketplace entry and package agree on the version. It says a project runs a release as published when every server the plugin starts installs from that release's tag. Nothing ties the enabled plugin's manifest version to the release whose tag the servers install from. So a project can satisfy AXM-pinned-and-rooted ('runs it as one release published it') through an earlier release while its manifest names a later one. The scenario is a version bump that missed the server pins. It satisfies both premises and breaks the first clause of the claim. I checked the escape: if 'the plugin's manifest' in DEF-release meant the enabled plugin's manifest, only 0.5.3 would be a release and the scenario would break AXM. But DEF-release's own wording ('a release', 'one release') treats releases as many, one per tag, which supports the reading under which the scenario holds.

counterexample: Missing premise (both parts needed): 'The release a project runs is the one whose version the manifest of the plugin it enabled names, and every server that plugin starts is part of the harness and reads the declarations and ledger of the project that enabled it.'
reasoning: Two steps of the derivation rest on facts no premise states. (1) The derivation says 'that release is the code at the tag of the one version the plugin's manifest names'. DEF-release defines releases per tag, and 'runs a release as published' checks only the servers' install tag, so the enabled manifest's version is never linked to that tag. (2) The derivation says 'so each server is pointed at that project'. AXM-pinned-and-rooted says the harness reads that project's declarations and ledger. No premise says the harness is exactly the set of servers the plugin starts, or that each server, rather than the harness as a whole, reads only that project. A plugin that starts one server pointed at its own install directory, beside servers that read the project, satisfies AXM-pinned-and-rooted as worded. The declared-test clause does follow from AXM-pinned-and-rooted ('runs that project's tests in that project's environment').

The premises fit both outcomes. A plugin pinned correctly to its own manifest's tag satisfies them with the claim true. The recorded scenario, a manifest at 0.5.3 with servers from tdlp--v0.5.2, satisfies them with the claim false. A single misdirected server does the same for the 'pointed at the project' clause. The premises are too weak to decide the claim.

Attacks: (1) A branch's derivation rule cites C1 (supported) and C2 (insufficient). The policy requires supported, and the branch is adopted. For AXM-design-rests-on-measurement to hold, C2 must not be 'a measurement the design cites'. But a contract the derivation rule names as evidence is, on any natural reading, cited by the design, and then AXM's third clause forbids adoption. The scenario only survives by splitting the derivation rule's citations from the design's, which is the unstated bridge, recorded as the gap. (2) A negative design asserts that some approach fails and cites a contract that reads refuted. That measurement agrees with the design, so AXM rejects nothing; the decision is only not adopted. The claim says refuted 'rejects the decision'. This turns on whether 'reads refuted' means 'contradicts it', which no premise says. In this framework contracts are naturally stated positively, so I record it as part of the gap rather than as a realizable failure. (3) Aggregate reading: the design's measurement is the weakest state across its contracts, by analogy with DEF-contract-state across slices. With a policy that requires exactly 'insufficient', C1 supported and C2 insufficient aggregate to insufficient, and the branch is adopted while C1 does not read 'that state'. This needs a policy that rejects supported evidence for being too strong, which is contrived, but it shows the premises do not fix how several contracts combine. No scenario survives as a falsification under the natural bridge. All three turn on the bridge.

counterexample: Missing premise: 'A branch is a design; the measurement it cites is every contract its derivation rule names as evidence, each read on its own by DEF-contract-state; it agrees with the branch only when each such contract reads in the state the policy requires, and a cited contract that reads refuted contradicts it.'
reasoning: The premises speak of 'a design' and 'the measurement it cites' (singular), and DEF-contract-state reads one contract across its slices. Neither mentions branches, derivation rules, several cited contracts, or what makes a measurement 'contradict' a design. The derivation's first step, 'A contract a branch's derivation rule cites is the measurement the design cites', is asserted, not derived. The step from 'reads refuted' to 'contradicts the design', which is needed for 'rejects the decision', is also unstated. With the bridge below the claim follows clause by clause from AXM-design-rests-on-measurement: agreement required, contradiction rejects, and absent, unreadable or other-state blocks adoption. Without it, the claim's terms are not linked to the axiom's.

With the distributive bridge above, the claim follows. With the aggregate bridge (the design's measurement reads as the weakest of its contracts) and a policy requiring a state below supported, NOT(claim) follows: the branch is adopted while some cited contract reads in a state other than the required one. With a negative design, a refuted contract agrees with the design, so AXM does not make it reject, and the claim's 'rejects the decision' is not derived. The premises pick none of these readings, so they are too weak to decide the claim.

subject: BRN-consistency-declarations-gate
text: Not a defect in this claim, but worth the author's look: under DEF-premise-graph and DEF-proof-state, a staged lemma X that is never committed can be cited by a declared branch Y, and Y becomes PROVEN with X carrying load. Only roots have to be declared axioms or definitions. So an unapproved proposition can sit inside an approved branch's proof. If that is not intended, DEF-proof-state needs a clause such as 'every node a declared node depends on is declared'. Separately, 'that branch keeps its proof state' would read more tightly as 'losing its subject leaves its proof state unchanged'.

subject: DEF-current-trial
text: Two observations on the legacy clause, neither turned into a trial. (1) 'The build when it was made' is a fixed historical fact at the premise level. Recovering it in practice needs the head revision as it was at that moment, so a history rewrite that makes that commit unreachable leaves the clause well-defined but unrecoverable. (2) Restating DEF-current-trial itself (this change) can alter which legacy trials count as current even on nodes that do not depend on DEF-current-trial. BRN-falsification-trial-ledger's 'stops being current only when...' holds with DEF-current-trial fixed, which the claim implicitly assumes. (3) For LMA-blast-radius-propagation: under a revert (r restated back to content a dependent was verified against), the dependent's old trial becomes current again with no re-verification after the modification. The lemma does not claim otherwise, but its closing remark ('this is the invalidation AXM-blast-radius-invalidation requires') rests on reading 're-verified' as 'verified against this content'.

subject: BRN-goal-guard
text: Design weaknesses the premises allow, and which are not counterexamples because the claim inherits the definitions: (1) DEF-agent-commit identifies the agent only by the Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer. An agent commit without the trailer is 'the human's': it is not refused, it ends any open report, and it approves every policy goals.yaml declares. (2) DEF-goal-set covers only files named on a test's run line or in reads:. A helper a declared test imports without naming it is outside the goal set. (3) Any later human commit that touches any goal-set file ends the report and approves every policy, including one an agent added. The negation trial records the separate tension between AXM-commit-is-approval and judging a pending commit.

reasoning: Attacks tried, with both premises held. (1) A server notices that a working-tree declaration file differs from the head revision and appends an event to the ledger, either through a watcher or on a later read. A verdict is computed from ledger events, for example a policy held while that event stands. Every verdict is still computed from committed content and the ledger, DEF-ledger holds, and the edit has changed a verdict. This is not a refutation because AXM-commit-is-approval's 'from no other file in the working tree' can be read as forbidding any flow from that file into a verdict, including a flow through the ledger. Under that reading the scenario breaks the axiom. I recorded it as the entailment gap instead. (2) Checking out another branch rewrites the declaration file without a commit. It also moves the head revision, so it is a revision change, not an edit to a file. Out of scope. (3) Editing an untracked or new declaration file: no declaration at the head revision changes. (4) Editing the ledger itself: DEF-ledger says a declaration file is not part of it. (5) Legacy trials judged by the declarations committed when they were made: that content is committed and the edit leaves it alone. (6) An evidence-named commit: a commit is immutable. No scenario survived in which every premise unambiguously holds.

counterexample: Missing premise: no server writes a ledger entry that is derived from, or triggered by, an uncommitted declaration file, apart from evidence a run records. Alternatively: AXM-commit-is-approval's 'from no other file in the working tree' also excludes such a file reaching a verdict through the ledger, not only directly.
reasoning: The step 'by DEF-ledger a declaration file is not part of the ledger, so the edit adds no entry to it either' does not follow. A file not being part of the ledger does not mean nothing appends to the ledger in response to that file. DEF-ledger lists events among the records and does not say what an event may record or what triggers one. AXM-commit-is-approval limits what a verdict is computed from, not what the servers write into the ledger. The lemma itself concedes that ledger content can depend on the working tree (evidence a run records), so the axiom is read as a limit on direct inputs only. Under that reading, a ledger entry written from an uncommitted declaration file, by a watcher or by a read that logs a worktree difference, carries the edit into a verdict. The carve-out names a commit and a run's evidence. It does not name a server-written event or note.

NOT(claim) would need some uncommitted edit that changes a verdict or a proof state. AXM-commit-is-approval rules out the direct route. The indirect route through the ledger is left open by the premises (the gap above) but no premise asserts that any server takes it. NOT(claim) is therefore not derivable.

Attacks tried. (1) One evidence record is recorded against two contracts: C1, which no declared test can measure, and C2, which declared test T measures. By DEF-belief-eligible the record is belief-eligible: it is measured and recorded against a contract (C2) that a declared test can measure. AXM-no-belief-write-path then lets it move a measured belief, even C1's, because no premise ties eligible evidence to the belief over the contract that made it eligible. If 'recorded against a contract that no declared test can measure' covers any contract the record names, clause 2 fails. Under the natural singular reading (one contract per record) the record falls outside the claim, so this is not a refutation. I recorded it as the entailment gap. (2) Tense: evidence is recorded while T is declared, then T's declaration is removed and committed, and the evidence keeps holding C's posterior. The claim and DEF-belief-eligible use the same relative clause, so whichever revision 'declared' is read at, they stay aligned. Not a refutation. (3) An uncommitted declaration reaching the belief model: AXM-commit-is-approval says it takes no effect. A test run that reads the working-tree file produces evidence, and that is not the declaration taking effect. (4) An uncommitted edit changing a verdict: excluded by LMA-worktree-inert as cited.

counterexample: Missing premise: every evidence record is recorded against exactly one contract (or: evidence moves only the posterior of the contract it is recorded against). Secondarily: every belief in the belief model is a posterior over a contract slice.
reasoning: Clause 1 follows from AXM-commit-is-approval. Clause 3 is LMA-worktree-inert, weakened to verdicts. Clause 2 does not follow as stated. DEF-belief-eligible makes a record eligible when it is recorded against 'a contract that a declared test can measure'. The claim excludes all evidence 'recorded against a contract that no declared test can measure'. These are complements only if each record is recorded against exactly one contract, and no cited premise says so (DEF-belief-eligible fixes exactly one provenance per record, not one contract). A second, smaller gap: AXM-no-belief-write-path covers 'a measured belief, the posterior over a contract slice', but the claim says 'a belief'. That step holds only if every belief the model holds is such a posterior.

NOT(claim) would need one of three things. An uncommitted declaration taking effect is excluded by AXM-commit-is-approval. An uncommitted edit changing a verdict is excluded by LMA-worktree-inert. Evidence against an unmeasurable contract moving a belief would need multi-contract records or a non-posterior belief, and no premise asserts either. None is derivable.

Attacks tried. (1) A staged lemma L, never committed, is cited by a branch B declared at the head revision. DEF-premise-graph admits both, and by DEF-proof-state B can be proven with L inside its proof. Does L 'take effect as a declaration'? The premises separate declared from staged only in the grounding clause, where roots must be declared axioms or definitions. AXM-commit-is-approval also lets the ledger feed proof states. So L acts as ledger content, not as a declaration. The broader reading, where any graph role counts as effect, would contradict DEF-premise-graph for every admitted staged proposal, so it is not the claim's meaning. No failure. (2) One commit drops a branch's subject and also restates the branch: the trials are set aside and the proof state changes, but the restatement causes that. The claim means losing the subject alone changes nothing, and the subject is not an input: it is not an edge (DEF-premise-graph), not part of a fingerprint (DEF-current-trial), and excluded by name (DEF-proof-state). (3) The same id declared twice at the head revision: one version goes unused. Nodes are identified by id, though, and the node is admitted, so AXM-no-silent-failure and the claim, both phrased per node, still agree. (4) A staged proposal for an id that is declared: it is never a candidate, and the node for that id is the declared one. Consistent. (5) Build order: admission is monotone, nothing is ever removed, and a build ends only at the fixpoint. The admitted set is therefore the unique closure, so 'no build admits' is the same as 'cannot take its place in the premise graph'. No scenario survived.

(a) The graph's only inputs are those DEF-premise-graph names: declarations at the head revision and proposals staged in the ledger. (b) By AXM-commit-is-approval a declaration takes effect only from the committed revision. A staged proposal is not from it, so it takes no effect as a declaration. This matches DEF-proof-state, where only declared axioms or definitions ground a proof. (c, d) AXM-no-silent-failure, with 'no build admits' equal to 'cannot take its place' because the build's admitted set is unique. (e) DEF-proof-state excludes the subject. DEF-current-trial's fingerprint depends only on statement and cited premises. DEF-premise-graph makes only citations edges. So losing the subject changes neither the branch's place nor which trials are current. I found no unstated assumption. One weakness: clause (b) is thin. The cited premises name only one effect a staged proposal lacks (grounding), so the clause promises little beyond that.

NOT(a) would need another source of nodes, which contradicts DEF-premise-graph. NOT(b) would need a staged proposal to count as declared, and the only 'declared' test in the premises (grounding in DEF-proof-state) rules that out. NOT(c, d) contradicts AXM-no-silent-failure. NOT(e) would need the subject to be an input to the proof state, which DEF-proof-state excludes by name. None is derivable.

Attacks tried. (1) A policy requires supported. The branch's rule names two contracts, one reading supported and one insufficient. If 'it agrees with the design when every one of them reads in the state the design's policy requires' gives only a sufficient condition, the axiom never says this mixed measurement fails to agree. Adoption is then not excluded, and the claim's 'adopted only while every contract reads in that state' fails. Under the definitional reading (agrees exactly when) the scenario is excluded. This is not a refutation, and I recorded it as the gap. (2) A policy requires 'no evidence', which DEF-contract-state lets a slice-less contract read. Such a contract is in the required state, so the claim's 'with no evidence ... short of adoption' would clash with agreement. However, the axiom's 'absent' plausibly covers a no-evidence measurement, and the claim lists 'no evidence' apart from states. Not decisive. (3) A derivation rule that names no contract: the claim only gives a necessary condition, which holds vacuously, and asserts no adoption. No failure. (4) The required state is refuted: the second sentence excludes that case, and the first still matches the axiom. (5) A contract with mixed slices reads as its weakest slice under DEF-contract-state. Consistent.

counterexample: Missing premises: (i) every branch is a design, the state a policy criterion requires of a branch's evidence is the state its design's policy requires, and a decision on the branch is that design's adoption; (ii) a design's cited measurement agrees with it ONLY when (exactly when) every contract its derivation rule names reads in the state the policy requires.
reasoning: There are two unstated steps. (i) The derivation opens with 'A branch is a design'. It also treats 'a policy criterion that requires a branch's evidence in a state' as 'the state the design's policy requires', and 'the decision' as the design's adoption. Neither cited premise says a branch is a design or relates a policy criterion to a design's policy. AXM-design-rests-on-measurement speaks only of designs. (ii) The first sentence and the 'another state' clause need the necessity direction: the measurement agrees only when every cited contract reads in the required state. The axiom says it 'agrees with the design when' every one does. This ledger writes 'exactly when' where it means a biconditional (DEF-current-trial, DEF-proof-state), so a plain 'when' gives a sufficient condition only. Nothing cited then excludes agreement while some named contract reads in another state. The refuted clause needs neither step, because it uses the axiom's 'contradicts it when' in its stated direction.

NOT(claim) has three possible forms. A refuted contract not rejecting contradicts the axiom's 'contradicts ... is rejected'. Adoption while some named contract reads otherwise would need an affirmative premise that such a measurement agrees, or that adoption follows from something; the premises give adoption only necessary conditions, so this is not derivable. Adoption with no evidence or an unreadable contract contradicts 'absent or cannot be read is not adopted'. NOT(claim) is not derivable. The premises are too weak to entail the claim (the gap), but they do not entail its negation.

Attacks tried. (1) The agent commits a change to the goal set without the trailer. By DEF-agent-commit that commit is the human's, so it is not 'an agent commit'. By AXM-goal-set-is-human it even approves every policy the goal set declares. That is a weakness in the design, but outside this claim, which covers only agent commits. (2) A human commit that carries the trailer is an agent commit by definition and is refused. Consistent with the claim. (3) An agent commit removes the test that names file F and edits F in the same commit. DEF-goal-set counts tests declared before or after the commit, so the commit still changes the goal set and is refused. (4) The human's next commit to the goal set has nothing to do with the agent's change. The report ends anyway, and by the axiom that commit approves whatever policy the agent added. The claim only says 'until the human next commits the goal set', so it still holds. (5) 'A human' named as approver versus the axiom's 'the human': the claim's necessary condition is weaker than the axiom's, so it follows. (6) A tension in the premises: 'Only the human changes the goal set', together with DEF-goal-set (a commit changes the goal set when it changes such a file), is contradicted by any agent commit 'made anyway'. So every world in which all premises hold contains no such commit, and the report and approver clauses hold vacuously there. I found no world that satisfies the premises in which the claim fails.

The claim restates AXM-goal-set-is-human clause by clause: refused; reported until the human next commits the goal set; and while reported, an adoption under a policy goals.yaml declares does not stand as approved unless the human is named as approver. The claim's 'needs a human named' is implied by that. DEF-agent-commit fixes which commits are the agent's. DEF-goal-set fixes which files count and when a commit changes them, including the before-or-after test rule. AXM-commit-is-approval fixes that 'declared in goals.yaml' means at the head revision. One loose step in the derivation: it reads the axiom's 'takes effect only from the committed revision' as 'takes effect from' it. The claim does not depend on that step. I found no unstated assumption.

NOT(claim) would need an agent commit to the goal set that is not refused, a made-anyway commit that goes unreported before the human's next goal-set commit, or an adoption that stands approved without a named human approver while one is reported. Each contradicts a clause of AXM-goal-set-is-human. The tension in attack (6) makes the premises entail that no made-anyway agent commit exists, which makes the claim vacuous in part, but it does not derive the claim's negation.

Attacks tried. (1) One server installs from the tag. Another installs from a published package of the same version built from that tag, or from the commit the tag points to. If DEF-release's 'A project runs that release as it was published when every server the plugin starts installs from that tag' gives only a sufficient condition, AXM-pinned-and-rooted can still hold, since the project runs the code at the tag as published. The claim's 'every server installs from the tag' then fails. Under the definitional biconditional reading the scenario breaks AXM-pinned-and-rooted. This is not a refutation, and I recorded it as the gap. (2) The plugin is enabled at user scope and at project scope, at different versions. A server of the other version means the project does not run the named release as published, which breaks AXM under the biconditional reading. Not a valid counterexample. (3) The tag is moved after publication. Installing from the tag still meets DEF-release, so the claim holds literally. (4) The manifest, marketplace and package versions disagree. DEF-release asserts they are one version, so the scenario breaks a premise. (5) A declared test run by hand from the harness: the claim's last clause is unrestricted, while the axiom covers only tests that a plugin server runs. Read in context, no failure.

counterexample: Missing premise: DEF-release states the necessity direction, that a project runs the release as it was published ONLY when (exactly when) every server the plugin starts installs from the tag tdlp--v<version>. Secondarily: the claim's 'a declared test runs' is limited to runs made by a server the plugin starts.
reasoning: The derivation's step 'running it as published means every server the plugin starts installs from that tag' uses the necessity direction of DEF-release's 'A project runs that release as it was published when every server the plugin starts installs from that tag'. As written, that sentence states a sufficient condition. This ledger writes 'exactly when' where it means a biconditional (DEF-current-trial, DEF-proof-state), so the plain 'when' cannot be taken as one. Without the necessity direction, AXM-pinned-and-rooted's 'runs the release ... as it was published' says nothing about how each server installs, and the claim's first clause does not follow. The rest does follow. 'Pointed at the project that enabled it' comes from 'measures that project: it reads that project's declarations and ledger'. The test clause comes from 'runs that project's tests in that project's environment, not in the harness's own', which the claim should limit to runs made by a server the plugin starts.

NOT(claim) has three possible forms. A server not pointed at the enabling project contradicts AXM-pinned-and-rooted's 'measures that project'. A server-run declared test running in the harness's environment contradicts 'in that project's environment, not in the harness's own'. A server installing from somewhere other than the tag is left open under the sufficient reading but is asserted by no premise. NOT(claim) is not derivable.

subject: AXM-goal-set-is-human
text: Noticed while verifying BRN-goal-guard; carries no proof weight. Read literally, 'Only the human changes the goal set' together with DEF-goal-set ('a commit changes the goal set when it changes such a file') is contradicted by any agent commit 'made anyway'. So any world satisfying the axiom contains no such commit, and the axiom's report and approver clauses, and BRN-goal-guard's, are never exercised in a world where the premises hold. Two smaller points. First, by DEF-agent-commit a trailer-less agent commit is the human's, and under this axiom it approves every policy goals.yaml declares. Second, any human commit to the goal set, even one unrelated to the agent's change, ends the report and approves what the agent added. A restatement such as 'only the human's commit approves a change to the goal set' would remove the contradiction. That is the author's call.

subject: DEF-proof-state
text: Noticed while verifying BRN-declarations-gate and BRN-consistency-declarations-gate; carries no proof weight. (1) As stated, 'proven' requires grounding roots that are declared axioms or definitions, plus the node's own current trials. It does not require that a lemma the node cites is proven. So BRN-declarations-gate can become PROVEN while its premise LMA-worktree-inert stays DOUBTED, unless something outside this definition enforces otherwise. (2) A branch declared at the head revision can be proven through a staged lemma that was never committed, because DEF-premise-graph admits it and only grounding roots must be declared. If adoption is meant to rest only on committed content (AXM-commit-is-approval: 'commit is approval'), no cited premise currently says that a declared branch whose proof passes through a staged proposal cannot support a decision.

reasoning: I tried to make an edit alone move a verdict or proof state while keeping both premises. (1) The edited declaration file sits outside the working tree. The axiom's last clause does not exclude it, but its first sentence lets no declaration take effect except from the committed revision, so the edit reaches nothing. (2) The declaration file doubles as a captured artifact or links into the ledger. DEF-ledger says no declaration file is part of the ledger, so this scenario breaks a premise. (3) A declared test reads the declaration file, so the edit would make its contract stale. Staleness is computed from the head revision and the commits that evidence names, and the edit touches neither. Running the test appends a record, which 'nothing else' excludes. (4) A server rereads its inputs when a working-tree timestamp changes. It rereads the same head revision and ledger. (5) Inputs that are not files, such as the clock or the environment. The edit does not change them, so any change they drive is not caused by the edit. (6) A pre-fingerprint trial is judged by 'the declarations committed when it was made'. Those are fixed by history the edit does not touch. No scenario keeps both premises and lets the edit alone move a verdict or proof state.

By AXM-commit-is-approval, every verdict and proof state is computed from committed content (the head declarations, the commits evidence names, and the declarations committed when a pre-fingerprint trial was made) and from the ledger, and from no other working-tree file. The scenario fixes 'no commit' and 'no appended record'. An edit moves no revision, so committed content is unchanged. DEF-ledger keeps the declaration file out of the ledger, so the ledger is unchanged too. 'Computed from' is read in its ordinary sense, as a function of those inputs; that is not an extra premise. A declaration file outside the working tree is covered by the axiom's first sentence rather than its last clause, so 'every input is what it was' holds even though the rule cites only the second sentence. I checked that the closing sentence excludes a later commit or record rather than assuming one away. No unstated assumption found.

NOT(claim) needs some verdict or proof state to depend on a declaration file's working-tree content, or needs the edit to change committed content or the ledger. The axiom excludes the first. The scenario excludes the second. DEF-ledger keeps the file out of the ledger. I also looked for an inconsistency in the premises that would let anything follow. Reading the ledger from the working tree is allowed by 'and from the ledger', and DEF-ledger's 'append-only' clashes with nothing in the axiom. NOT(claim) is not derivable.

Attacks tried with all four premises kept: (1) An agent commits a goal-set change without the trailer. DEF-agent-commit makes it the human's commit, so it is not an agent commit and the claim is untouched. The guard's notion of identity rests only on the trailer (noted). (2) The agent edits a file a declared test reaches only indirectly, such as a module its script imports or a file under a directory its run line names. That file is outside the goal set as DEF-goal-set draws it, so the claim is silent here, not false. (3) One agent commit drops a test and edits the file it named. It changes the goals file itself, and DEF-goal-set's before-or-after rule counts the named file too. (4) The agent moves a policy out of the goals file into another declaration file, and an adoption under that policy stands without the human. The axiom and the claim both speak only of policies the goals file declares, so the claim holds; this is a limit on the guard's reach (noted). (5) The named approver is a human but not 'the human'. The claim's 'needs a human named' is a necessary condition that the axiom's 'unless the human is named' implies. (6) An adoption made before the agent commit. 'While one is reported no adoption ... stands' covers it, and so does the claim. (7) A human commit that leaves the goal set alone ends the report under neither text. No attack keeps the premises and breaks the claim.

Checked clause by clause against AXM-goal-set-is-human. 'An agent commit that would change the goal set is refused' gives the first sentence; 'changes' and 'would change' pick out the same commit. 'One that is made anyway is reported until the human next commits the goal set' gives the second sentence word for word. 'While one is reported no adoption under a policy the goals file declares stands as approved unless the human is named as its approver' gives the third. The claim's 'a human' is weaker than 'the human', and 'needs' is read as 'needs in order to stand as approved'. DEF-agent-commit and DEF-goal-set fix which commits and which changes the terms pick out. The claim uses those terms in the same words as the axiom, so no reading can split the two. The claim does not need AXM-commit-is-approval. The rule's use of it (a policy takes effect from the committed revision) is consistent with the axiom's distinction between a policy taking effect and being approved. No unstated assumption.

I looked for an inconsistency in the premises that would let NOT(claim) follow. (a) A commit that is 'refused' yet 'made anyway' is the axiom's own bypass case. The refusal is the guard's answer, so there is no contradiction. (b) A refusal is judged on a change that is not yet committed. AXM-commit-is-approval computes every verdict the servers report from committed content and the ledger only. No premise says the refusal is a verdict the servers report, so the two premises do not collide (noted). (c) The opening sentence, 'the human's commit of the goal set approves it ... and no other commit does', agrees with the agent case: an agent commit approves nothing and is reported. (d) DEF-agent-commit splits commits into two classes, so no commit is both the agent's and the human's. NOT(claim) is not derivable.

counterexample: Take two branches, B1 and B2, where only B1 is a design. AXM-design-rests-on-measurement says a design is a branch; it does not say every branch is a design. B2's derivation rule names a contract C, which reads insufficient by DEF-contract-state. A decision on B2 under a policy criterion that requires supported adopts B2. The axiom gates designs and says nothing about B2, and DEF-contract-state holds, so every premise holds. The claim says B2 is adopted only while C reads supported, yet B2 is adopted while C reads insufficient. This refutes the claim only if 'A design is a branch' runs one way. Read as an identity, B2 is a design and the scenario breaks the axiom.
reasoning: Within designs, every clause held against these attacks: (1) The required state is refuted. The claim's 'where that state is not refuted' exempts this case. (2) The required state is insufficient and a contract reads supported. The axiom and the claim both demand the required state itself, so the stronger state blocks adoption under both texts (a design consequence, noted). (3) The rule names no contract. The claim's 'only while' is then vacuous, and the axiom's 'absent' keeps the design unadopted, so the two do not clash. (4) The required state is 'no evidence' and every contract reads no evidence. The measurement agrees but is absent, so the design is not adopted, which matches the claim's 'with no evidence ... short of adoption'. (5) One contract reads refuted and another cannot be read. The design is rejected, and so also not adopted. The one scenario that survives depends on how the axiom's opening is read. I record it as inconclusive and name the missing premise under entailment.

counterexample: The claim, and the rule's 'By AXM-design-rests-on-measurement a branch is a design', need every branch decided under a policy criterion to be a design. The axiom states only the converse, 'A design is a branch'. Needed premise: every branch is a design. For example, the axiom could open 'A branch is a design, and a design is a branch'.
reasoning: Every other step follows. The criterion's required state is the design's policy's state. The measurement agrees exactly when every named contract reads in that state, each contract read by DEF-contract-state. 'Adopted only while it agrees' gives the first sentence. 'Contradicts exactly when one reads refuted where the required state is another', together with 'contradicted means rejected', gives the second. 'Does not agree, is absent or cannot be read means not adopted' gives the third: a contract with no evidence reads 'no evidence', which makes agreement false or the measurement absent, and either way the design is not adopted. The gap is the subject: the axiom gates designs, and the claim gates every branch.

NOT(claim) needs one of three things: a branch adopted while a named contract is not in the required state; a refuted reading that does not reject; or an off-state, empty or unreadable reading that still allows adoption. For designs the axiom forbids all three. For a branch that is not a design the premises are silent. That makes the claim underivable (the entailment gap) but does not derive its negation, because no premise says such a branch exists or is adopted. I also checked the axiom for an internal clash. With no contract named, 'agrees' holds vacuously while 'absent' forbids adoption, and the claim's 'only while' fits either reading. NOT(claim) is not derivable.

counterexample: The release bundles its own set of declared self-check tests. Each server the plugin starts installs from the tag of the manifest's version, reads the enabling project's declarations and ledger, and runs that project's tests in that project's environment. It also reads the bundled set and runs one of those declared tests in the harness's own environment. AXM-pinned-and-rooted holds: the server measures that project and runs that project's tests where the axiom says. DEF-release holds as well. The claim fails, because a declared test a server runs is running in the harness's environment. This refutes the claim only if a server may read declarations other than the project's. If 'measures that project' is exclusive, the scenario breaks the axiom.
reasoning: These attacks failed: (1) A server keeps running an install cached from an earlier tag after an upgrade. AXM-pinned-and-rooted, with DEF-release's 'exactly when', forces every server onto the current manifest's tag, so the scenario breaks a premise. (2) The plugin starts a server that is not part of the release. The same biconditional forces it onto the tag too. (3) A test's run line switches into the harness's interpreter. The axiom says that project's tests run in that project's environment. (4) The tag is moved after publication. DEF-release counts installing from the tag as running the release as published, and the claim asserts only the install. (5) The plugin is enabled for the user rather than by a project. The claim and the axiom both speak only of the project that enabled it. The one scenario that survives depends on whether a server reads only the project's declarations. I record it as inconclusive and name the missing premise under entailment.

counterexample: The claim's 'a declared test any of them runs' is wider than the axiom's 'that project's tests'. The rule's 'so a declared test any of them runs runs there' needs every declared test a server runs to be one of that project's tests. Needed premise: the only declarations a server reads are that project's (equivalently, every test a server runs is one of that project's tests).
reasoning: Clause 1 follows. AXM-pinned-and-rooted says the project runs the manifest's release as published, and DEF-release's 'exactly when' turns that into every server installing from the tag of the manifest's version. Clause 2 follows if 'pointed at' is read as 'reads that project's declarations and ledger'. Clause 3 holds only for that project's tests. The axiom says what a server reads, not that it reads nothing else, while the claim covers every declared test a server runs.

NOT(claim) needs one of three things: a server not installed from the tag, a server pointed at another project, or a declared test run in the harness's environment. The first two contradict the premises outright. The third is consistent with the premises (the inconclusive scenario) but is not entailed, because no premise says a server reads declarations other than the project's. I also checked DEF-release's statement that the manifest, the marketplace entry and the package name the same version. It constrains scenarios but cannot yield NOT(claim). NOT(claim) is not derivable.

counterexample: Besides the posterior over each contract slice, the belief model holds a belief over a component, computed from every record filed against that component's contracts. An imported record, with its source, artifact and hash, is recorded against contract C, which no declared test can measure. The record is therefore not belief-eligible. It enters C's slices alone, and the component belief, which reads C's slices, moves. AXM-no-belief-write-path holds, because no posterior over a contract slice changed. DEF-belief-eligible, DEF-evidence-record, AXM-commit-is-approval and LMA-worktree-inert hold as well. The claim fails: evidence against a contract no declared test can measure moved a belief. This refutes the claim only if the belief model holds beliefs other than posteriors over contract slices. If 'a belief' means a measured belief, the scenario falls outside the claim.
reasoning: Within posteriors over contract slices I could not break clause 2. (1) A record is imported against a contract no declared test measures, and a later commit declares a test for it. If both DEF-belief-eligible and the claim are read at the same revision, the record is either outside the claim (the contract is now measurable) or still ineligible. The revision is left open (noted). (2) An ineligible import shares an artifact hash with a measured record and displaces it. That would change a posterior through evidence that is not eligible, which AXM-no-belief-write-path forbids. (3) A record counts toward a second contract. DEF-evidence-record forbids this. (4) A contract declared only in the working tree receives evidence through the ledger. Its declaration does not take effect, so no declared test measures it and its records are ineligible. Clause 1 held: a declaration committed only at an old revision is still 'committed'. Clause 3 held, since LMA-worktree-inert is stronger. The scenario that survives depends on 'a belief' reaching past posteriors over contract slices. I record it as inconclusive and name the missing premise under entailment.

counterexample: Clause 2 concludes 'moves a belief' from AXM-no-belief-write-path, which governs only 'a measured belief, the posterior over a contract slice'. The rule drops 'measured'. Needed premise: every belief in the belief model is a posterior over a contract slice, or is computed from such posteriors alone. Otherwise clause 2 should be restated as 'moves no measured belief'.
reasoning: Clause 1 follows from AXM-commit-is-approval's first sentence, with 'reach the belief model' read as 'take effect in it'. Clause 3 is LMA-worktree-inert without 'and no proof state'. Clause 2: DEF-evidence-record puts the record in its one contract's slices. DEF-belief-eligible makes it ineligible when no declared test measures that contract, read at the same revision for both, as the shared wording warrants. AXM-no-belief-write-path then leaves every posterior over a contract slice unchanged. That argument reaches measured beliefs only; the claim says 'a belief'.

NOT(claim) needs one of three things. An uncommitted declaration takes effect: AXM-commit-is-approval forbids it. A lone edit changes a verdict: LMA-worktree-inert forbids it. A record against an unmeasurable contract moves a belief: for a posterior over a contract slice AXM-no-belief-write-path forbids it, and for any other belief the premises are silent, which is consistent with the scenario but does not entail it. I also checked whether AXM-no-belief-write-path clashes with removing a test. If eligibility were re-judged at the head revision, a commit removing a contract's last test would change its posterior without any evidence. That strains DEF-belief-eligible's time index but forces no instance of NOT(claim). NOT(claim) is not derivable.

subject: BRN-declarations-gate
text: DEF-belief-eligible does not say at which revision 'a contract that a declared test can measure' is judged. There are two options. (a) At the head revision, where AXM-commit-is-approval computes every verdict. Then a record imported against a contract no test measured starts moving that contract's belief as soon as a later commit declares a test. Clause 2 still holds, since the contract is now measurable, but a pre-loaded record goes live. Also, a commit that removes a contract's last test would make its records ineligible and so change the posterior with no evidence, which goes against AXM-no-belief-write-path. (b) At the revision the record is made. Neither problem arises. Fixing the revision in DEF-belief-eligible would remove both problems. I did not record this as a gap because the claim and the definition use the same wording, and reading both at one revision entails clause 2.

subject: BRN-design-gate-reads-evidence
text: The axiom and the claim both require every named contract to read in the required state itself. A stronger state does not count. So under a policy whose criterion requires insufficient, a contract reading supported leaves the design short of adoption. If policies are meant to accept evidence stronger than they require, the axiom needs 'in the required state or a stronger one', and the claim should follow it.

subject: BRN-goal-guard
text: These observations do not break the claim, but they limit what the guard covers. (1) An agent commit is identified only by its trailer. An agent commit without the trailer counts as the human's and approves the goal set. (2) DEF-goal-set covers only files a declared test names on its run line or in reads:. It misses modules the test's script imports and files under a directory the run line names. (3) The before-or-after rule applies to declaring a test but not to tracking a file. A commit that starts tracking a file a declared test already names changes the goal set only if 'git tracks' is read after the commit. (4) The approver clause covers only policies the goals file declares. An agent commit that moves a policy into another declaration file takes that policy out of the guard. (5) Naming the human as approver is not the same as the human approving. (6) A refusal is judged on an uncommitted change, but AXM-commit-is-approval computes every verdict the servers report from committed content and the ledger. If the servers are what refuses, that input is not on the axiom's list.

reasoning: Strongest attack: a record that sets a measured trial aside, either an amendment by an agent or an event the server appends itself on finding the trial's artifact damaged. Both are asserted under DEF-belief-eligible because they are neither measured nor imported. After the record is appended, the slice's posterior no longer counts the trial, so an asserted record has changed a measured belief. The attack fails against AXM-no-belief-write-path. The change is caused by appending a record that is not belief-eligible, so it is a change through something other than belief-eligible evidence. For the agent's amendment, the axiom's zero-weight clause also excludes it. The scenario survives only if 'changes only through belief-eligible evidence' is taken to mean just that the posterior is some function of the eligible records, whatever else decides which of them count. On that reading the axiom would exclude almost nothing, so I do not hold the premise to it. I also tried two other attacks. First, an asserted note that prompts a run whose measured record then moves the belief: the belief moves through the measured record, the note's content carries no weight, and the posterior is the same as if the run had been prompted any other way. Second, an asserted record that changes the declarations in effect: that is outside the scope the axiom and the claim share, so it is a counterexample to neither.

The step uses two cited facts and nothing else. DEF-belief-eligible says every record carries exactly one provenance, and a record that is neither measured nor imported is asserted. So an asserted record is not belief-eligible, and no fact about its contract, artifact or author is needed. AXM-no-belief-write-path says that, under the declarations in effect, a measured belief changes only through belief-eligible evidence. The claim is the instance of that axiom for asserted records, under the same scope, and 'measured belief' means the same thing in both (the posterior over a contract slice). I checked whether 'cannot change' claims more than 'changes no belief through'. Under the axiom's 'only through', a change caused by a record is a change through that record, so the two mean the same and no premise is missing.

NOT(claim): under the declarations in effect, some record with provenance asserted changes some measured belief. Deriving it needs one of two things. Either an asserted record is belief-eligible, which DEF-belief-eligible's exactly-one-provenance rule and its residue clause exclude. Or a measured belief moves through something that is not belief-eligible, which AXM-no-belief-write-path excludes. The only remaining route is an asserted record that changes the declarations themselves, and that lies outside the scope both the premise and the claim are stated in. The negation is not derivable.

One attack per clause. Clause (c): a contract with declared compatibility key {python}, T1 at 3.11 and T2 at 3.12. They differ on the key, so DEF-contract-slice puts them in different slices. I looked for anything that is a measured belief and holds both. A contract-level reading over its slices is not a posterior. AXM-no-belief-write-path makes a measured belief the posterior over one slice, and DEF-contract-slice computes it from that slice's trials and the declared prior alone, with nothing from another slice entering it. If a human derives a prior by hand from T2's slice and then declares it, it enters as a declaration, which is the frame the axiom is scoped to, not as T2. If a commit drops python from the key, T1 and T2 share a slice, but then they no longer differ on the declared key, so the clause's antecedent fails. Clause (b): two slices of 6 trials each under a declared sufficiency of 10, which would be 12 if pooled. DEF-contract-slice counts sufficiency over each slice's own trials, so both are below it and AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict withholds a verdict. The 'insufficient' label is the labelled estimate that axiom allows, not a verdict. Clause (a): an asserted amendment that rewrites a trial's key value, moving it between slices and changing two posteriors. LMA-asserted-is-inert forbids an asserted record from changing any measured belief. None of these attacks survives.

Clause by clause. (a) 'Changes only through belief-eligible evidence' is AXM-no-belief-write-path applied to a slice, which the axiom names (a measured belief is the posterior over a contract slice). 'Never through an asserted record' is LMA-asserted-is-inert. Both are stated under the same scope as the claim. DEF-contract-slice agrees independently: the posterior is computed from the slice's trials, which are belief-eligible by definition, and the declared prior. (b) DEF-contract-slice makes each slice a claim whose sufficiency is counted over its own trials, and AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict withholds a verdict below the declared sufficiency for a claim. (c) DEF-contract-slice's membership condition (the same value for every key in the declared compatibility key) separates trials that differ. AXM-no-belief-write-path makes a measured belief one slice's posterior, and DEF-contract-slice computes it from that slice alone. Clauses (b) and (c) drop the 'under the declarations in effect' scope, but each refers to a declared sufficiency or a declared key, which the current declarations supply, so no scope assumption is hidden. A slice with no declared sufficiency makes clause (b) vacuous in the premise and the claim alike.

NOT(claim) needs one of four things. A slice posterior moving through something not belief-eligible contradicts AXM-no-belief-write-path. A slice posterior moving through an asserted record contradicts LMA-asserted-is-inert. A verdict from a slice below its declared sufficiency contradicts AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict, since DEF-contract-slice makes a slice a claim. One posterior computed from trials with two key values contradicts DEF-contract-slice's membership condition together with 'nothing from another slice entering it'. None of these can be derived from the premises.

Attacks tried. (1) A reader that moves the head revision while producing its output, for example by checking out the base it compares against and leaving it there, without editing a declaration file. The premise graph is built from the declarations at the head revision, so the graph could differ. This fails. If the declarations at the new head differ, the report has changed the declarations, which DEF-report excludes. If they are the same, the graph, every statement and every fingerprint are unchanged. (2) Rewriting old history so that a legacy trial's 'build when it was made' is different. DEF-current-trial ties that build to when the trial was made, a fact about the past that no later act can reach. (3) Deleting a trial or rewriting a damaged artifact while producing the report. DEF-ledger makes the ledger append-only, and DEF-report forbids appending. (4) A posterior re-estimated stochastically each time a report computes it. That would change a measured belief without belief-eligible evidence, which AXM-no-belief-write-path excludes. (5) A caller who reads 'evidence is stale' and re-runs a test. The belief then moves through the measured record that run appends, not through the report. None of these attacks survives.

Beliefs: DEF-report says producing a report appends no record and changes no declaration, so the declarations in effect are the same before and after, and AXM-no-belief-write-path governs the whole interval. Belief-eligible evidence is a trial record (DEF-belief-eligible), and the trial records the servers keep are the ledger (DEF-ledger). None is appended, so no measured belief moves. Proof states: DEF-proof-state lists the inputs (the node's place in the premise graph; the version the build admitted, with its statement, cited premises and declared sufficiency; and the trials recorded on it) and excludes everything else. DEF-premise-graph builds the graph from the declarations at the head revision and the proposals staged in the ledger, and neither changes. The trials on a node are unchanged: none is appended, and none can be removed from an append-only ledger. DEF-current-trial's three conditions depend on validity after amendments (no amendment is appended), membership of the graph (unchanged) and fingerprints. Fingerprints are determined by statements and premises, which are unchanged; for legacy trials they come from the build when the trial was made. The step depends on one reading: 'changes no declaration' means the declarations at the head revision are the same afterwards. That is the plain meaning, and it also covers a head moved to a revision with different declarations.

NOT(claim) requires some input to a measured belief or a proof state to differ after the report. The declarations cannot differ (DEF-report). Ledger records cannot differ: DEF-report forbids appending, and DEF-ledger forbids anything but appending. Nothing else can differ: AXM-no-belief-write-path rules it out for beliefs, and DEF-proof-state's exhaustive list of inputs together with DEF-current-trial's three conditions rules it out for proof states. The negation is not derivable.

Attacks tried. (1) The plugin is enabled at user scope and used in a project that never enabled it itself, so 'the project that enabled it' has no referent. But the claim inherits AXM-pinned-and-rooted's own quantifier ('a project that enables the plugin'), so whichever reading of 'enables' makes the axiom apply makes the claim apply in the same way, and vice versa. (2) The tag is moved after publication, or dependencies are left unpinned and resolved at install. The server still installs from the tag, which is all the claim says. The weakness is in DEF-release's account of 'as published', not in this step. (3) A server that reads only the enabling project's declarations and ledger but appends its own records to a ledger kept elsewhere. The derivation takes 'pointed at' to mean the axiom's 'the only declarations and ledger it reads are that project's', and on that reading the claim holds. A server that wrote to a foreign ledger and also read it would break the axiom's 'reads' clause, so the premise excludes the realistic version of this misconfiguration. (4) The plugin is enabled at two versions at once. The axiom would then require every server to install from two tags, so the premises cannot all hold and the scenario refutes nothing. None of these attacks survives.

'Installs from the tag of the version the manifest names': AXM-pinned-and-rooted says the enabling project runs the release the manifest names, as it was published. DEF-release says that release is the code at tdlp--v<version> for the manifest's version, and that a project runs it as published exactly when every server the plugin starts installs from that tag. That biconditional gives this conjunct directly. 'Pointed at the project that enabled it': this is the axiom's 'measures that project and no other: the only declarations and ledger it reads are that project's', which is the content the derivation gives to 'pointed at'. 'A declared test any of them runs runs in that project's environment, not the harness's own': a declared test a server runs is one of the tests it runs, and the axiom places those in that project's environment, not the harness's. No step needs an uncited fact.

NOT(claim): some server the plugin starts installs from somewhere other than that tag, or reads another project's declarations or ledger, or runs a declared test outside the project's environment. The first contradicts AXM-pinned-and-rooted through DEF-release's biconditional. The second and third contradict the axiom's second sentence directly. The negation is not derivable.

Attacks tried. (1) Timing, clause two: an imported record R is recorded against contract C at a revision where no declared test measures C. A later commit declares a test for C, R becomes belief-eligible, and C's posterior moves with no new record. That is evidence recorded while C was unmeasurable now moving a belief. The attack fails on the clause's present tense: 'a contract that no declared test can measure' is judged when the belief moves, and C is measurable then. The move itself comes from a committed declaration, which AXM-commit-is-approval lets take effect. The attack would succeed only if measurability were fixed at the moment of recording, which the clause does not say. (2) Clause one: a server that reads an uncommitted declaration in order to warn that the working tree differs from head. The declaration reaches the server but not the belief model, whose verdicts AXM-commit-is-approval computes from committed content and the ledger and from no other file in the working tree. (3) Clause one: a declaration-like item staged in the ledger. By AXM-commit-is-approval, a declaration takes effect only from the committed revision. (4) Clause two: a record against the unmeasurable contract C1 that also moves the measurable contract C2. DEF-evidence-record confines the record to C1's slices, and it is not belief-eligible in any case. (5) Clause three: an edit followed by an automatic commit is not 'and nothing else'. None of these attacks survives.

Clause one is AXM-commit-is-approval's first sentence, with 'reaches the belief model' read as 'takes effect in it'; the axiom's second sentence makes this concrete for every verdict and proof state. Clause two: DEF-evidence-record ties a record to exactly one contract and that contract's slices. DEF-belief-eligible makes the record belief-eligible only if that contract is one a declared test can measure. AXM-no-belief-write-path, under the declarations in effect, lets nothing else move a posterior. The claim leaves out the axiom's scope 'under the declarations in effect', but its antecedent (a contract that no declared test can measure) is itself judged against the declarations in effect, so the scope is carried and no assumption is hidden. Clause three is LMA-worktree-inert restricted to verdicts.

NOT(claim) needs one of three things. An uncommitted declaration taking effect contradicts AXM-commit-is-approval. A record against an unmeasurable contract moving a posterior under the declarations in effect contradicts AXM-no-belief-write-path together with DEF-belief-eligible and DEF-evidence-record. A working-tree edit alone changing a verdict contradicts LMA-worktree-inert. None of these can be derived.

Attacks tried. (1) A derivation rule that names no contract. 'Every named contract reads in the required state' then holds vacuously, so the first sentence permits adoption without asserting it, and AXM-design-rests-on-measurement's 'absent' blocks it. No clause fails. (2) A required state of refuted. The second sentence is restricted to 'where that state is not refuted', and the first sentence follows. (3) One contract reads refuted and another cannot be read. The design is rejected and not adopted, which is compatible with both clauses. (4) A decision under a criterion that requires something other than the design's policy. The axiom identifies the two. (5) A policy that requires the state 'no evidence', with one named contract that has no slice.
