By DEF-contract-state that contract reads no evidence, which is the required state, so the axiom's agreement condition holds and nothing reading refuted contradicts it. The design is kept from adoption only if that contract makes the cited measurement 'absent'. The axiom's text allows both that reading and the opposite one. Because the scenario does not hold on every reading of the premise, I record it as the entailment gap and the negation result rather than as a refutation.

counterexample: Missing premise; either of these closes it: (a) the state a policy criterion requires is a slice state (refuted, stale, contested, insufficient or supported) and never 'no evidence'; or (b) a design one of whose named contracts reads 'no evidence' has an absent cited measurement. Neither AXM-design-rests-on-measurement nor DEF-contract-state states either.
reasoning: When the required state is one of the slice states, every clause follows. A contract reading refuted where another state is required contradicts the design, which the axiom rejects. A contract reading another state, no evidence, or nothing readable leaves the measurement not agreeing, so the design is not adopted. What does not follow is the clause 'one [reading] with no evidence ... leaves the decision short of adoption' when the required state is itself 'no evidence'. DEF-contract-state gives 'no evidence' as the state a contract with no slice reads in, and neither premise forbids a policy from requiring it. The contract then reads in the required state, so the measurement agrees. The derivation holds the design back by calling that contract's measurement 'absent'. But the axiom defines the cited measurement as each named contract, each read on its own, so a contract read as 'no evidence' is a measurement that is present and has been read. 'Absent' can just as well mean that the rule names no contract, which is the case 'absent' is otherwise needed for, since agreement is vacuous there.

Take a criterion requiring 'no evidence' and one named contract that has no slice. An argument for NOT(clause) can be built from the axiom's words just as well as the derivation's argument for the clause. The measurement agrees, since every named contract reads in the required state. Nothing reads refuted, so nothing contradicts it. The contract was read, so it can be read. The measurement consists of that reading, so it is not absent. No non-adoption condition applies, and adoption stays open, which is the negation of 'leaves the decision short of adoption'. The derivation's argument for the clause depends on 'absent' covering that contract. The premises do not decide which argument holds.

Attacks tried. (1) A server runs a declared test, stores the artifact, computes its hash, takes the record's metrics from the artifact, and appends a measured record that holds neither the artifact (nor a reference to it) nor the hash. Every part of DEF-belief-eligible's description of measured provenance is met, the record moves belief as AXM-no-belief-write-path allows, and 'carries' fails. (2) A contract is scored on metric m, a measured record's artifact lacks m, and the posterior counts the missing m as a failure. The record's own metrics all came from its artifact, the belief moves through that eligible record, and 'excluded rather than synthesised' fails. (3) An artifact holds correct=9 and total=10, and the record carries accuracy=0.9: the metric is taken from the artifact but not contained in it. Each attack holds on one reading only. Attack (1) holds unless 'captured its artifact with the artifact's hash' is read as saying the record holds them. That is how the derivation takes it, and the parallel description for imported ('brought in with ... an artifact and the artifact's hash') suggests it. Attack (2) holds unless 'changes only through belief-eligible evidence' is read as 'through the metrics eligible records carry', which is the derivation's reading. Because the premises allow the readings that defeat these attacks, I record what is missing as the entailment gap and the negation result, not as a refutation.

counterexample: Missing premises: (a) a measured record holds the artifact the server captured, or a reference that resolves to it, together with that artifact's hash; (b) a measured belief is computed from the metrics that belief-eligible records carry and from nothing else, so no value is supplied for a metric a record lacks. Neither DEF-belief-eligible nor AXM-no-belief-write-path states either. Premise (b) would also need to say whether a metric computed from the artifact's contents counts as contained in it.
reasoning: Two steps depend on facts that no cited premise states. (1) 'So every measured record carries both': DEF-belief-eligible says how a measured record comes about (the server ran a declared test, captured its artifact with its hash, and took the record's metrics from it). It says nothing about what the record holds afterwards, and 'carries' is a property of the record's content. (2) 'Scoring it anyway would move a measured belief through something that is not belief-eligible evidence': belief-eligibility is a property of records, and a value supplied for a metric that an eligible record lacks belongs to no record. AXM-no-belief-write-path says which records may move a posterior, not that a posterior reads a record only through the metrics it carries. The clause also leaves open whether a metric computed from what the artifact holds counts as contained in it.

From the same premises, an argument for NOT(claim) is as good as the derivation's argument for the claim. DEF-belief-eligible constrains what the server did to produce a measured record, so a measured record may hold no artifact and no hash and still be measured. AXM-no-belief-write-path is satisfied when a posterior that supplies a value for a missing metric moves through an eligible record, so a missing metric may be synthesised. The derivation's argument relies on the opposite readings of the same two premises. The premises decide neither conjunct.

subject: LMA-asserted-is-inert
text: This lemma relies on the natural reading of AXM-no-belief-write-path. On that reading, no record that DEF-belief-eligible classes as asserted may set a measured record aside and so move a posterior. That includes an amendment, a note, or an event the server appends itself. If any part of the design stops counting evidence found damaged or mis-recorded by appending such a record, it conflicts with this lemma, and nothing declared says how damaged evidence stops counting. Separately: DEF-belief-eligible makes any import that comes with a source, an artifact and a hash belief-eligible, whoever made the artifact, while the axiom gives an agent's statement zero weight. Nothing declared distinguishes an import whose artifact an agent wrote by hand.

subject: BRN-plugin-pinned
text: 'Pointed at the project' is grounded only through what a server reads: AXM-pinned-and-rooted says 'the only declarations and ledger it reads are that project's'. Nothing declared says where a server appends its records. A server that read the project's ledger but appended its records somewhere else would satisfy the axiom. If 'pointed at' is meant to cover writes as well, the axiom should say so. Also, DEF-release treats 'as published' as the same thing as 'installs from the tag', so a tag moved after publication, or dependencies resolved unpinned at install, still count as running the release as published.

subject: BRN-declarations-gate
text: Clause two of the claim has no scope, while AXM-no-belief-write-path is scoped to the declarations in effect. I judged 'a contract that no declared test can measure' at the moment the belief moves, and on that reading the clause follows. If the clause is meant to be judged at the moment the evidence is recorded, it fails. An import recorded against a contract with no declared test becomes belief-eligible once a test for that contract is declared, and it then moves the posterior with no new record. The author may want to state which reading is intended, or add 'under the declarations in effect' as LMA-asserted-is-inert and BRN-model-honest now do.

reasoning: I tried six scenarios, each checked against both premises. (a) Required state supported; C1 reads supported and C2 has no slice, so it reads no evidence. DEF-contract-state now says a criterion never requires no evidence, so C2 is not in the required state. AXM's measurement does not agree, so the branch is not adopted, which is what the claim says. Before the restatement this was the opening: a criterion could require no evidence. That opening is closed. (b) Required state refuted and C1 reads refuted. The claim's rejection sentence is guarded by 'where that state is not refuted', and its first sentence allows adoption only while C1 reads refuted, matching AXM. (c) Required state insufficient and C1 reads supported, which is stronger than required. AXM's 'reads in the required state' means equality, so the measurement does not agree and the branch is not adopted. The claim's 'another state than the required one' says the same, so this is consistent even if it is odd as design. (d) The derivation rule names no contract. AXM's 'every one reads in the required state' holds vacuously, but the measurement is absent, so the branch is not adopted. The claim only states necessary conditions and blockers and never asserts adoption, so nothing fails. (e) Required state supported, C1 reads refuted and C2 cannot be read. AXM's measurement contradicts the design, so it is rejected. The claim also says rejected, and its 'short of adoption' for C2 is compatible because rejection implies non-adoption. (f) The rule names an id that is not a declared contract. Neither AXM's measurement ('each contract its derivation rule names') nor the claim's 'such contract' quantifies over it, so they agree. None of these satisfies every premise and breaks the claim.

Sentence 1 follows from two AXM clauses: 'adopted only while the measurement agrees' and 'agrees exactly when every one reads in the required state'. AXM also says the criterion's required state is the policy's single state. Sentence 2 follows from AXM's 'contradicts exactly when one reads refuted where the required state is another' together with 'a design whose cited measurement contradicts it is rejected'. Since AXM identifies adoption with a decision on the branch under the criterion, the claim's 'rejects the decision' says the same as 'the design is rejected'. Sentence 3 has three cases, each ending in non-adoption: (i) A reading in another state means not every contract reads in the required state, so there is no agreement. (ii) 'No evidence' is a contract's reading when it has no slice (DEF). Since DEF says the required state is always one of the five slice states, a no-evidence reading differs from it, so there is no agreement. This step needs exactly the sentence DEF now adds. (iii) A contract that cannot be read reads in no state, so it does not read in the required state; AXM's 'cannot be read ... is not adopted' also covers it. I looked for an unstated premise, such as several required states, an order-based 'at least' reading, or refuted not being a reading a contract can take. DEF makes refuted the weakest state, so a contract can read refuted. Neither premise needs anything beyond what it states.

NOT(claim) would need one of three derivations: (1) adoption while some named contract reads outside the required state, (2) no rejection when a contract reads refuted and the required state is not refuted, or (3) adoption with a no-evidence or unreadable reading. (1) and (3) are blocked because AXM makes agreement necessary for adoption and defines agreement as every contract in the required state, and DEF removes no evidence from the states a criterion can require. (2) is blocked because AXM makes contradiction sufficient for rejection. The one slack spot is the zero-contract case: AXM gives vacuous agreement but also an absent measurement. That resolves to non-adoption, which the claim does not deny. NOT(claim) is not derivable.

I tried five scenarios against all three premises. (a) The test declares passed, the run writes 'latency' but not 'passed' into the artifact, the exit code is 0, and the contract's rule reads passed. DEF-measured-record falls back to the exit code only 'when the run wrote none'. The record therefore carries latency only, lacks passed, and is excluded with no value supplied. The claim says the same. (b) The run writes passed=true into the artifact and exits non-zero. By DEF the metrics are those written, so passed=true comes from the artifact. The claim says metrics come from that artifact, so they agree. This is a design property, not a failure of the claim. (c) The run writes no metrics and the test does not declare passed. The record carries no metric, any rule that reads a metric excludes it, and the claim agrees. (d) An exit-code record set against DEF-belief-eligible's gloss that measured provenance 'took the record's metrics from that artifact'. If the exit code is outside the artifact, no measured record with an exit-code metric can satisfy both definitions, so the scenario breaks a premise and refutes nothing. If the exit code counts as part of the artifact, the claim holds. (e) A measured record without an artifact hash is ruled out directly by DEF-measured-record. No scenario satisfies every premise and breaks the claim.

Each clause of the claim is DEF-measured-record's matching clause, stated equally or more weakly. 'Carries a reference to the artifact the server captured and its hash' is DEF's sentence 1 without 'from the run'. 'Metrics come from that artifact, or from the captured exit code for a passed-declaring test whose run wrote none' is weaker than DEF's 'are those the run wrote ... its only metric is passed, read from the exit code'. 'Excluded, never given a value' is DEF's 'excluded, and no value is supplied for it'. The claim therefore follows from DEF-measured-record alone, with no unstated premise. The derivation rule's second sentence does not hold as written, though it is not needed for the claim. 'By DEF-belief-eligible such a record is belief-eligible' would need two things. First, the metrics must be taken from the artifact; the exit-code case satisfies this only if the captured exit code counts as part of the artifact, which no premise says. Second, the record must stand against a contract a declared test can measure, which DEF-measured-record does not state. AXM-no-belief-write-path and DEF-belief-eligible ground the branch but play no part in deriving it.

NOT(claim) would need one of three: (1) a measured record without an artifact reference or hash, (2) a measured record whose metrics come from somewhere other than the artifact or, in the passed fallback, the exit code, or (3) a record that lacks a rule-read metric yet is scored with a supplied value. DEF-measured-record states the opposite of each, and DEF-belief-eligible and AXM only narrow further: metrics from the artifact, and belief moved only by eligible records. The premises do conflict in one place. DEF-belief-eligible's artifact-only metrics clash with DEF-measured-record's exit-code fallback when the exit code lies outside the artifact. That conflict only forces exit-code metrics to count as artifact-derived, or such records not to exist. The premises do not assert that such a record exists, so no derivation of NOT(claim) follows.

subject: BRN-runner-captures
text: Verifier observations with no proof weight. (1) The claim is almost word for word DEF-measured-record, so its proof is definitional. It shows the claim agrees with the definitions. Whether the runner actually produces such records is the implementer's evidence (CTR-surface-intact), not this proof. (2) The derivation rule's step 'By DEF-belief-eligible such a record is belief-eligible' is not entailed, though the claim does not need it. DEF-belief-eligible describes measured provenance as 'took the record's metrics from that artifact'. DEF-measured-record's exit-code fallback reads 'passed' from 'the exit code the server captured' when the run wrote nothing into the artifact. Unless the captured exit code counts as part of the artifact, the two definitions disagree on that case. Exit-code records would then fail to be measured under DEF-belief-eligible, and by its exactly-one-provenance rule they would be asserted, carrying no weight under AXM-no-belief-write-path. DEF-belief-eligible also requires a contract that a declared test can measure, which DEF-measured-record does not state. If exit-code records are meant to move beliefs, DEF-belief-eligible should admit metrics read from the captured exit code. Any node that depends on exit-code records being belief-eligible currently has no stated ground for it. (3) A design property the definition implies: a run that writes passed=true into its artifact and exits non-zero is recorded as passed, because the exit code is read only when the run wrote no metric.

subject: BRN-design-gate-reads-evidence
text: Verifier observation with no proof weight. AXM-design-rests-on-measurement and the claim both read 'reads in the required state' as equality, not as 'at least as strong as' in DEF-contract-state's order. A policy that requires insufficient or contested would therefore block adoption once a cited contract becomes supported. The claim correctly entails this from its premises. If the author meant 'required state or stronger', the axiom needs restating. Also, when the derivation rule names no contract, agreement holds vacuously and only AXM's 'absent' clause blocks adoption. That is consistent, but it rests on reading 'absent' as covering an empty citation.

reasoning: Attacks tried, each holding both premises: (1) An asserted amendment marks a measured record invalid, so it drops out of its slice and the posterior moves. Under AXM-no-belief-write-path that is a belief change through a record that is not belief-eligible, which the axiom forbids. DEF-belief-eligible decides eligibility only from the record's own provenance, the way it was captured or imported, and whether a declared test can measure its contract. It never depends on another record, so no asserted record can change what is eligible. (2) An asserted record is later relabelled measured or imported. DEF-belief-eligible defines measured by how the record was made (the server ran a declared test and captured the artifact with its hash) and imported by how it was brought in (source, artifact, hash). A relabel meets neither, so by the closing sentence the record stays asserted. (3) Relay: an agent's assertion is re-entered as an imported record whose artifact the agent wrote. The record that moves the belief is a separate record with provenance imported. The asserted record still moves nothing, so the claim survives. (4) The restated exit-code branch: it applies only to provenance measured, where the server captured the exit code, so an asserted record cannot reach it. (5) A decision record changes the declarations in effect. That falls outside AXM's scope and the claim's alike, because both carry the same 'under the declarations in effect' qualifier. No scenario holds both premises and has an asserted record moving a measured belief.

Chain: DEF-belief-eligible says every record carries exactly one provenance and eligibility needs measured or imported. An asserted record is therefore neither, so it is not belief-eligible. AXM-no-belief-write-path says that under the declarations in effect a measured belief changes only through belief-eligible evidence. So an asserted record changes none. Two possible hidden steps were checked. (a) 'record X changes belief' is the same as 'belief changes through X'. That is the sense of AXM's 'through', and a joint update where an asserted record works alongside an eligible one is still a change partly through a non-eligible record, which AXM excludes. (b) The scope qualifiers are word for word the same in premise and claim. The DEF-belief-eligible restatement (passed taken alone from the captured exit code) only widens how a measured record gets its metrics. It leaves the provenance partition unchanged, so the step still holds.

NOT(claim) would need an asserted record that is belief-eligible, or a route to a measured belief other than eligible evidence. DEF-belief-eligible rules out the first and AXM-no-belief-write-path the second. The premises are consistent: take a model where each slice posterior is computed only from measured or imported records against contracts a declared test can measure. Both premises hold there and no asserted record has any effect. With consistent premises the negation is not derivable.

Attacks tried, each holding all four premises: (a) A contract has two slices, each below sufficiency, and a contract-level verdict is issued on their pooled trials. That verdict is not one a slice issues (DEF-contract-slice: the verdict a slice issues is on that slice). The pooled posterior is not a measured belief either, because AXM-no-belief-write-path defines a measured belief as the posterior over a contract slice. So the claim as written does not fail. The weakness is logged as a wording note. (b) A human derives the contract's prior from slice A's trials and declares it, and slice B's posterior uses that prior. DEF-contract-slice allows the declared prior as an input. No trial from A enters B as data, so trials are not pooled. (c) A commit narrows the compatibility key, so trials that differed under the old key now share a slice. The claim is headed 'Under the declarations in effect' and refers to the declared key. Under the key in effect those trials do not differ. (d) One trial carries a value for a key and another carries none. DEF-contract-slice needs the same value for every key, so they never share a slice. (e) An asserted amendment moves a trial into another bucket or changes its key value, which shifts a posterior. That is a change through a record that is not belief-eligible, which AXM-no-belief-write-path and LMA-asserted-is-inert both forbid. None of these holds every premise while making a clause fail.

Clause 1: AXM-no-belief-write-path identifies a measured belief with the posterior over a contract slice and limits its changes to belief-eligible evidence under the declarations in effect. LMA-asserted-is-inert, now proven, excludes asserted records. Clause 2: DEF-contract-slice makes each slice a claim of its own, with sufficiency counted over its own trials. AXM-sparse-data-no-verdict, instantiated with that slice as the claim, gives no verdict below the slice's declared sufficiency. I checked whether 'its declared sufficiency' assumes a slice-level declaration no premise supplies. It names the same object as the axiom's 'declared sufficiency for a claim', and where none is declared the axiom and the clause are vacuous together. Clause 3: by DEF-contract-slice, trials that differ on a compatibility-key value fall in different slices, and a posterior is computed only from its own slice's trials and the declared prior. Since AXM defines a measured belief as one slice's posterior, no measured belief combines them. No step needs an uncited fact.

NOT(claim) would need one of three things: a non-eligible or asserted route to a slice posterior, a verdict below sufficiency, or two key-differing trials in one slice. Each contradicts a cited premise. I checked the premises for a hidden inconsistency that would make anything derivable. The candidate is AXM-no-belief-write-path's 'a statement by an agent or a human carries zero weight' against DEF-contract-slice computing the posterior from the declared prior, which a human writes. AXM scopes itself 'under the declarations in effect', which makes declarations the frame rather than statements. Even read the other way, 'zero weight' and 'computed from' clash only for an informative prior, so it is not a contradiction. The premises are consistent and the negation does not follow.

Attacks tried, each holding all five premises. Clause (a): staged proposals in the ledger do reach proof states, but they are not declarations. Declarations from 'the commits that evidence names' or from the revision a pre-fingerprint trial was made at are still committed content (AXM-commit-is-approval), so no uncommitted declaration takes effect. Clause (c): LMA-worktree-inert states it outright. An edit made on top of a declaration file that was never committed is still an edit with no commit, so it is covered. Clause (b), strongest attack: at revision R0, contract C has no declared test that measures it, and a record is imported against C with source, artifact and hash. At R1 a human commits a test that measures C. Under the declarations in effect at R1 the record is belief-eligible and moves C's slice belief. That refutes (b) only on the reading that judges 'no declared test can measure' at the time of recording. On the reading that judges it under the declarations in effect, C is measurable at R1, so the record is outside (b) and the clause holds. Under fixed declarations (b) follows: the record is not belief-eligible, so AXM-no-belief-write-path stops it from moving any belief. A scenario that refutes only one reading of an ambiguous clause is not a falsification. It is recorded as the entailment gap.

counterexample: Clause (b) needs either the qualifier, as in 'under the declarations in effect, no evidence recorded against a contract that no declared test can measure moves a measured belief', or a premise saying a record's eligibility is judged against the declarations at the revision it was recorded under, not at the head. Without either, this holds every premise: at R0 contract C is declared and no declared test measures it, and a record is imported against C with its source, artifact and hash. At R1 a human commits a test that measures C. Under the declarations in effect at R1 the record is belief-eligible (DEF-belief-eligible), enters C's slice (DEF-evidence-record) and moves its measured belief (AXM-no-belief-write-path allows this). Evidence recorded against a contract no declared test could measure has moved a measured belief.
reasoning: Clauses (a) and (c) follow, (a) from AXM-commit-is-approval's first sentence (reading 'reach the belief model' as 'take effect') and (c) from LMA-worktree-inert. Clause (b) does not follow as written. Its only premise about belief movement, AXM-no-belief-write-path, holds 'under the declarations in effect', and the derivation rule carries that qualifier in its middle step. The claim then drops it. From 'under D, P' one cannot conclude an unqualified P, and this branch is about declarations changing by commit, which is exactly when the unqualified reading matters. No premise says at which revision 'a contract that a declared test can measure' is judged. DEF-belief-eligible does not say, and AXM-commit-is-approval lets verdicts read both the head and the commits that evidence names.

NOT(claim) would need one of three things derivable: an uncommitted declaration taking effect, a record against a contract no declared test can measure moving a belief, or an edit alone changing a verdict. AXM-commit-is-approval, DEF-belief-eligible with AXM-no-belief-write-path, and LMA-worktree-inert rule these out in turn. The R0/R1 scenario shows that the negation of clause (b), read without its scope, is consistent with the premises. It does not show the negation follows, since nothing forces a test to be declared later. I checked the premises for a clash. DEF-evidence-record says every record 'enters the slices of that contract', while only eligible evidence moves a belief. Entering a slice and moving its belief are different things, so there is no contradiction and the negation is not derivable.

Attacks tried, each holding all seven premises: (1) The caller takes an audit report and imports it as a record against a contract a declared test can measure, with source, artifact and hash. The record is belief-eligible and moves a belief. But the caller appended it. Producing the report appended nothing (DEF-report), and the finding as output is still not a record, so the claim stands. (2) A report writes a non-declaration file into the repository. DEF-report forbids only ledger appends and declaration changes. Still, the proof-state inputs are head declarations and ledger proposals (DEF-premise-graph), the admitted version and the trials on it (DEF-proof-state), and validity, amendments and fingerprints (DEF-current-trial). Measured belief moves only through eligible evidence (AXM-no-belief-write-path). A non-declaration file is none of these. (3) A report moves the head revision or rewrites history. That changes the declarations at head or at a past revision, which 'changes no declaration' excludes. (4) A report appends an artifact. An artifact is neither a trial record with provenance nor a trial on a node. (5) A trial made before fingerprints is current or not by the build when it was made. That is a past fact a later report cannot change. (6) The graph is rebuilt on every read, so a different admission order might change the graph. I checked: admission only grows, a node goes in once all its premises are in, and a build ends only when every node left out cites a missing premise. The result is the least set closed under admission, so it does not depend on order. Rebuilding on the report's read gives the same graph. No scenario holds every premise and moves a belief or proof state.

Beliefs: DEF-report means producing a report appends no record of any provenance and changes no declaration. DEF-belief-eligible makes belief-eligible evidence a trial record with provenance, which is a record of the kind DEF-ledger names, so the report's output is not belief-eligible evidence and adds none. AXM-no-belief-write-path is scoped 'under the declarations in effect'. A report changes no declaration, so the declarations in effect are the same before and after, and dropping the qualifier in the claim is safe here. Proof states: the graph's inputs (DEF-premise-graph) are unchanged and the build is order-independent (see the counterexample trial). So the admitted version and its statement, premises and sufficiency are unchanged (DEF-proof-state). No trial or amendment is appended and no fingerprint changes, so the current trials are the same (DEF-current-trial). The proof state, which is computed from exactly these, is unchanged. Each step cites a premise.

NOT(claim) would need an input to a measured belief or a proof state that producing a report can change. Every such input in the premises (eligible ledger records, declarations, staged proposals, trials, amendments, fingerprints) is one that DEF-report excludes, or is fixed by the past. I checked the seven premises for a clash. DEF-report reads the repository but writes neither records nor declarations, DEF-ledger is append-only, and DEF-proof-state limits its inputs. They fit together in one model, a read-only renderer over an append-only log. So the negation is not derivable.

Attacks tried, each holding all three premises: (1) The test declares passed, the run writes latency but not passed, and the rule reads passed. DEF-measured-record falls back to the exit code only when the run wrote no metrics, so the record lacks passed, is excluded and is given no value. The claim says the same. (2) The run writes nothing and the test does not declare passed. The record has no metrics, so any rule that reads a metric excludes it. The claim agrees. (3) The run writes nothing, the test declares passed, and the rule reads both passed and latency. The record's only metric is passed, so it lacks latency and is excluded. The claim agrees. (4) A record labelled measured has no artifact reference, either from before capture existed or forged. DEF-belief-eligible makes measured mean the server captured the artifact with its hash. Such a record is not measured, and by its closing sentence it is asserted. DEF-measured-record gives every measured record the reference, so this is not a counterexample. (5) In the exit-code case, is passed 'given a value' that the record lacks? DEF-measured-record makes passed a metric the record carries, so the record does not lack it, and 'never given a value' still holds.

Each clause restates DEF-measured-record. 'Carries a reference to the artifact the server captured and that artifact's hash' is word for word the same. 'Its metrics come from that artifact' is weaker than 'are those the run wrote into that artifact'. The exit-code alternative has the same condition (the run wrote none and the test declares passed) and the same source (the exit code the server captured). 'Excluded, never given a value' matches 'is excluded, and no value is supplied for it'. 'Its contract's rule' presupposes a single contract, and the premise uses the same phrase. AXM-no-belief-write-path and DEF-belief-eligible are not needed for the step, but they agree: after the restatement DEF-belief-eligible names the same two sources under the same condition. No uncited fact is used.

NOT(claim) would need one of three things: a measured record with no artifact reference or hash, a metric from a third source, or a record lacking a metric that gets a supplied value. DEF-measured-record rules out each. The restatement could have opened a conflict between DEF-belief-eligible and DEF-measured-record. I compared them: both allow the artifact's metrics, or passed alone from the captured exit code when the run wrote none and the test declares passed. Neither allows anything else, so there is no conflict and the negation is not derivable.

subject: BRN-declarations-gate
text: Wording, not a trial: (1) No premise defines 'the belief model' in clause (a). I read 'reach the belief model' as 'take effect in', which AXM-commit-is-approval's first sentence covers. If 'reach' means 'is read by', no premise covers it, because AXM-commit-is-approval limits what verdicts and proof states are computed from, not what may be read. (2) DEF-evidence-record says every trial record 'enters the slices of that contract'. A slice (DEF-contract-slice, not cited here) holds only belief-eligible trials, so 'enters at most the slices of that contract' would avoid implying that ineligible records enter slices. (3) The clause (b) gap is closed by adding 'under the declarations in effect' to it, matching how LMA-asserted-is-inert and BRN-model-honest are scoped.

subject: DEF-belief-eligible
text: Wording, noticed while verifying LMA-asserted-is-inert and BRN-declarations-gate, not a trial: (1) The measured branch requires that 'the server ran a declared test' and that the record is 'recorded against a contract that a declared test can measure'. It never requires these to be the same test, so a run of a test that measures contract D, recorded against contract C, meets the text whenever some declared test measures C. (2) The imported branch requires a source, an artifact and its hash, but nothing about who wrote the artifact. An artifact an agent wrote, once imported, is belief-eligible here. Only AXM-no-belief-write-path's 'a statement by an agent or a human carries zero weight' keeps it from moving belief, so that clause carries real weight and is not decoration.

subject: BRN-model-honest
text: Wording, not a trial: (1) Clause 3 ('never pooled into one measured belief') holds because AXM-no-belief-write-path defines a measured belief as the posterior over one slice. It does not rule out a pooled contract-level estimate or verdict computed beside the slice posteriors, and no premise rules that out either. If the intent is 'no output pools key-differing trials', the claim and its premises need to say so. (2) AXM-no-belief-write-path's 'a statement by an agent or a human carries zero weight' sits next to DEF-contract-slice's posterior being 'computed from ... its contract's declared prior', and a human writes the prior. I read declarations as the frame ('under the declarations in effect') rather than as statements. Saying so explicitly would remove the tension.

subject: BRN-runner-captures
text: Design observation, not a trial: DEF-measured-record takes passed from 'the exit code the server captured' when the run wrote no metrics. No premise says the exit code is stored in the artifact whose hash the record carries. A hash check of the artifact therefore cannot confirm an exit-code-derived passed, and the audit trail for those records is weaker than for artifact-derived metrics. Saying where the captured exit code is kept, and whether a hash covers it, would close this.

subject: DEF-proof-state
text: Wording, noticed while verifying BRN-monitor-moves-nothing, not a trial: DEF-proof-state says a proof state is computed 'from nothing else belief.yaml or the ledger says about it'. Proof states belong to the design graph, whose declarations live in the consistency declarations file, not the component declarations file. Taken literally, the restriction does not reach the file the nodes are declared in. It made no difference to BRN-monitor-moves-nothing, because a report changes no declaration in any file, but the name looks like a slip.

reasoning: Split the claim into (a) only committed declarations reach the belief model, (b) under the declarations in effect a record against a contract no declared test can measure moves no measured belief, (c) an edit to a declaration file and nothing else changes no verdict, and attacked each. (b), strongest attack: commit X declares test T measuring contract C; the server runs T and records a measured record R against C that names X; a later commit Y, now HEAD, deletes T while C stays declared, so under Y no declared test can measure C. AXM-commit-is-approval lets verdicts be computed from 'the commits that evidence names', and X's content still declares T. So if R counted as eligible because T was declared at X, C's posterior could move and (b) would fail. This does not hold up. AXM-no-belief-write-path applies DEF-belief-eligible 'under the declarations in effect', and DEF-belief-eligible's eligibility condition is in the present tense ('a contract that a declared test can measure'), unlike the past-tense provenance clause 'ran a declared test'. Under Y, R is therefore ineligible, and the axiom forbids it from changing any posterior. Second attack: an imported record against C becomes eligible when a later commit declares a test for C, so C's belief moves across that commit. That crosses a change of declarations, and the claim's scope 'under the declarations in effect' excludes it. Third attack: R leaking into some other contract's slice. DEF-evidence-record rules this out (exactly one contract, its slices alone), and the axiom already forbids any belief change by an ineligible record. (a), attack: a declaration that is staged but not committed, or that lives in the ledger rather than the committed revision. AXM-commit-is-approval says a declaration takes effect only from the committed revision, so it takes no effect wherever it sits. Declarations committed at a non-HEAD revision (a commit that evidence names, or the revision a pre-fingerprint trial used) are still committed, so they do not refute 'only committed'. (c), attack: an edit that also rewrites an existing ledger line, or that is followed by a commit. Either one is more than 'nothing else'. Inside the stated condition, LMA-worktree-inert states (c) directly, and it also follows from AXM-commit-is-approval (computed from committed content and the ledger, no other working-tree file). No scenario keeps every premise true and breaks a conjunct.

(a) follows from AXM-commit-is-approval's first sentence: a declaration that takes effect only from the committed revision cannot reach the belief model uncommitted. Reading 'reach' as 'take effect in' is the only bridge, and it is the natural one. (b): for any record R, DEF-evidence-record fixes exactly one contract C. DEF-belief-eligible makes R eligible only if C is one a declared test can measure. Under the declarations in effect, the hypothesis says no declared test can measure C, so R is ineligible. AXM-no-belief-write-path says that under the declarations in effect a measured belief (the posterior over a contract slice) changes only through eligible evidence, so R changes none. The step I checked hardest is whether DEF-belief-eligible's 'a declared test' is judged against the same declarations as the claim's 'no declared test'. The definition carries no scope of its own, but the axiom invokes it under the prefix 'under the declarations in effect', and the claim now carries that same prefix. So both are judged against the same declarations, and no extra premise is needed. (c) is LMA-worktree-inert with 'and no proof state' dropped, which makes it a strictly weaker consequence. Each conjunct follows from the cited premises with no unstated assumption. The two residual readings (a definition left unscoped, and 'moves' versus 'changes') are wording, not a missing premise.

NOT(claim) needs at least one of three things. (i) An uncommitted declaration reaches the belief model, which contradicts AXM-commit-is-approval directly. (ii) Under the declarations in effect, a record against a contract no declared test can measure moves a measured belief. That record is ineligible by DEF-belief-eligible, and the movement contradicts AXM-no-belief-write-path. (iii) A declaration-file edit with no commit and no ledger append changes a verdict, which contradicts LMA-worktree-inert and AXM-commit-is-approval. So none of the three disjuncts can be derived. The premises are also mutually consistent: AXM-commit-is-approval's allowance for declarations at named or earlier commits does not clash with the HEAD-scoped eligibility in AXM-no-belief-write-path, because the latter is scoped to the declarations in effect. With consistent premises, they cannot entail the negation too.

subject: DEF-belief-eligible
text: Seen while verifying BRN-declarations-gate (no proof weight). (1) The definition's 'recorded against a contract that a declared test can measure' does not say which declarations 'declared' refers to. Today it gets its scope only when AXM-no-belief-write-path invokes it 'under the declarations in effect'. A later premise could cite the definition directly, without that axiom. AXM-commit-is-approval also lets verdicts read the commits that evidence names, whose declarations may differ from HEAD's. Writing 'a test declared in the declarations in effect' into the definition would close that off. (2) The definition does not require the test the server ran to be one that measures the contract the record is filed against. A measured record of test T' (which measures contract A) filed against contract B (measurable by some other declared test T) is eligible as written, and per DEF-evidence-record it enters B's slices. BRN-declarations-gate asserts nothing against this, so the branch is not affected. Any later claim that a measured belief reflects only the tests that measure its contract would need that tie stated.

reasoning: I tried six scenarios. Each kept every premise and tried to break the claim. (1) Shared artifact: a missing artifact has two records resting on it, R1 valid and R2 superseded. The axiom says the finding blocks while ANY resting record counts. The claim says it blocks 'while a record resting on that artifact or stamp counts', which is the same existential, so they agree. (2) Re-validation: R is quarantined, so it is set aside, the finding is information, and then an amendment restores R to valid. By DEF-set-aside, validity is read after the amendments, so R counts again. The axiom and the claim are both stated as states ('while' / 'once none does'), so the finding blocks again under both. No divergence. (3) A non-trial record rests on a damaged artifact. DEF-set-aside gives the set-aside condition only for trial records, but its last sentence ('a record that is not set aside counts') makes such a record count, so the finding blocks, as the claim says. When none counts, the contrapositive makes every resting record set aside, so 'naming why those records were set aside' is well-formed and names quarantined, invalid or superseded. (4) Mismatch read as 'audited and found altered' rather than 'can no longer be audited', which would put hash mismatches outside the axiom. I rejected this. The recorded contents can no longer be re-checked, so the derivation rule's classification is a fair reading, and the axiom's subject is damage. (5) Empty resting set: an artifact with a recorded hash but no record resting on it. 'Its recorded hash' presupposes a record, and the axiom's subject is 'a record's artifact or stamp', so this falls outside both. That is a scope wording issue, not a counterexample. (6) This was the strongest attack. The audit re-hashes only a subset of artifacts, for example a sample, or skips artifacts under set-aside records. A deleted artifact it never examines yields no finding and is never reported, which breaks the claim's first sentence. The scenario keeps the axiom only if 'a finding' means a conclusion the audit actually reached. Under the reading where 'No such finding is dropped' covers an unexamined damaged artifact, it violates the axiom. Because it keeps every premise on only one reading of a premise, and only exploits an omission rather than contradicting the blocking rules, I record it as the entailment gap and not as a falsification. No scenario kept every premise on an unambiguous reading and broke the blocking or reporting rule.

counterexample: The claim needs a coverage premise that no served premise states, for example: 'The audit re-checks every artifact and every stamp that any record rests on, whether or not that record counts, so every missing artifact, hash mismatch and untrusted stamp gives rise to a finding.' This could be a DEF of the audit's scope, or a clause added to AXM-damage-blocks-while-it-counts saying that each artifact or stamp that can no longer be audited yields a finding. Without it, the axiom only constrains findings that are made, not which damaged artifacts produce one.
reasoning: The blocking and reporting halves follow. Grant the derivation rule's classification: a missing artifact, a hash mismatch and an untrusted stamp are each an artifact or stamp that can no longer be audited. Then the axiom fixes the rest: blocks while any resting record counts; once none does, still reported with why those records were set aside, without blocking; never dropped. DEF-set-aside makes 'none counts' imply that every resting record is set aside, by the contrapositive of 'a record that is not set aside counts', so the reported reason is one of quarantined, invalid or superseded. That reason is read after the amendments. The opening sentence does not follow: 'The audit reports every artifact that is missing or no longer matches its recorded hash, and every stamp it cannot trust.' It ranges over artifacts and stamps. The axiom ranges over findings: 'a finding that ... can no longer be audited', 'No such finding is dropped'. Never dropping a finding once made is not the same as making one for every damaged artifact. Whether the audit examines every artifact and stamp that a record rests on, including those under set-aside records, can only be judged from the implementation. A secondary point that I did not count as a gap: no premise defines 'can no longer be audited'. Classifying the three conditions as such rests on the derivation rule, not on a premise. I judged it a fair unfolding, but a definition would make it explicit.

NOT(claim) has three disjuncts. (a) Some missing or mismatched artifact or untrusted stamp goes unreported. (b) Some such finding fails to block while a resting record counts. (c) Once none counts, such a finding is not reported as information naming why those records were set aside. Given the classification, (b) and (c) contradict AXM-damage-blocks-while-it-counts directly, and (c) also contradicts 'No such finding is dropped'. For (a), no premise asserts any omission or limit on what the audit examines. The premises are silent on coverage, which leaves that clause undecided (the entailment gap), but no derivation of an unreported damaged artifact exists. I also tested whether DEF-set-aside could let a set-aside record still count, which would yield a finding that never stops blocking. DEF states 'not set aside => counts' and 'set aside => moves no measured belief', but not 'set aside => does not count'. The claim is phrased in 'counts' throughout, though, so this ambiguity shifts when blocking stops under both the axiom and the claim alike and does not produce NOT(claim). NOT(claim) is not derivable.

subject: BRN-audit-blocks-what-counts
text: Wording notes from the verifier pass. These are not gaps and carry no proof weight. (1) The derivation rule says 'a record counts exactly when it is not set aside'. DEF-set-aside states only one direction ('a record that is not set aside counts'), plus 'a set-aside record moves no measured belief'. The converse holds only if 'counts' is identified with 'moves measured belief'. Stating 'a set-aside record does not count' in DEF-set-aside would make the 'exactly when' literal. (2) The derivation rule ends with 'so the audit judges a record by its amendments and not by the record alone', but the claim does not say this. If that property is meant to be verified, it belongs in the claim text. (3) 'Every artifact that is missing or no longer matches its recorded hash' is wider than the axiom's subject, 'a record's artifact or stamp'. Scoping it to 'every artifact or stamp a record rests on' would match the axiom and avoid the vacuous case where 'why those records were set aside' names an empty set. (4) The claim says the finding is 'reported as information', where the axiom says it 'does not block'. Saying 'and does not block' would make the equivalence explicit. (5) The derivation rule asserts that a hash mismatch is an artifact that 'can no longer be audited', but no premise defines that term. A DEF listing the conditions under which an artifact or stamp can no longer be audited would turn the classification into a cited step. (6) CTR-monitor-read-only is cited as evidence but is not a served premise, so it played no part in the judgement.

reasoning: Attacks tried, all with every premise held. (1) Mixed counting: artifact A has two records resting on it, R1 counts and R2 is quarantined; A's hash no longer matches. DEF-audit re-checks A (R1 and R2 rest on it, whether or not they count), so a finding arises; AXM makes it block because R1 counts. The claim says the same. No failure. (2) All set aside: R1 is later amended to superseded. By DEF-set-aside (both directions) R1 now does not count, so none does. AXM gives a non-blocking report with why R1 and R2 were set aside, and the finding is not dropped. The claim says the same. (3) Reinstatement: R1 is amended back to valid. Both AXM and the claim are stated over the current counting state ('while ... counts', 'once none does'), so the finding blocks again under both. (4) Vacuous 'none': a finding about an artifact no record rests on. This cannot arise, because DEF-audit only re-checks artifacts and stamps some measured or imported record rests on, so at least one record stands behind every finding. (5) Disagreeing stamp digests: two trials recorded different digests for one stamp. 'Can no longer be audited' is then ambiguous, but the claim uses DEF-audit's own predicate, so whichever reading is taken, it carries into both alike. (6) Scope (the strongest attack): R is a record that is neither measured nor imported, it rests on artifact A, and A is deleted. DEF-audit does not require A to be re-checked, so A may go unreported, which would break the claim's first sentence. I do not record this as a falsification. It is realizable only if some record outside 'measured or imported' rests on an artifact or stamp, and no premise says such a record exists. On a broad reading of AXM ('no such finding is dropped' read as covering every record's artifact) the scenario also fails. So the scenario shows the claim does not follow from the premises, not that the claim is false. It is recorded as the entailment gap.

counterexample: Main missing premise: every record that rests on an artifact or stamp is a measured or imported record. It could be added to DEF-audit. The other fix is to narrow the claim's first sentence to 'every artifact or stamp a measured or imported record rests on'. Weaker missing premise: when a re-check finds an artifact or stamp can no longer be audited, the audit makes a finding of it.
reasoning: The second sentence follows directly from AXM-damage-blocks-while-it-counts: it blocks while any record resting on the artifact or stamp counts, and once none does it is reported with why those records were set aside and does not block. DEF-set-aside (both directions) makes 'none counts' the same as 'all are set aside'. The first sentence does not follow as stated. It quantifies over 'every artifact or stamp a record rests on', but the only premise that makes the audit look at artifacts and stamps (DEF-audit) covers those that 'a measured or imported record rests on'. The derivation moves from 'measured or imported record' to 'record' without a premise to bridge them. AXM only governs a finding once it exists ('no such finding is dropped' assumes it was found), so AXM does not close the gap. The qualifier in DEF-audit suggests other kinds of record exist, and whether any of them rests on an artifact or stamp is exactly what the first sentence needs to know. A second, weaker point: DEF-audit says the audit 're-checks'. It never says a failed re-check produces a finding or report. The derivation's 'so every such artifact or stamp gives rise to a finding' supplies that step. This is close to definitional, but it is not stated.

NOT(claim) would need one of three things. (a) A finding that does not block while a record resting on it counts. This contradicts AXM. (b) A finding that blocks, or is reported without why its records were set aside, once none counts. This also contradicts AXM, and DEF-set-aside makes 'none counts' the same as 'all set aside', so no gap opens there. (c) An artifact or stamp a record rests on that can no longer be audited and goes unreported. For measured or imported records, (c) contradicts DEF-audit plus AXM's no-drop clause. For any other record it needs a premise saying such an artifact-bearing record exists, and none does. So NOT(claim) cannot be derived. The premises leave clause (c) open for records outside 'measured or imported', and that is recorded as the entailment gap, not as a second derivation.

subject: BRN-audit-blocks-what-counts
text: Context for the TRL-0296 gap. Other parts of the graph declare a record provenance outside 'measured or imported': LMA-asserted-is-inert names records with provenance asserted. So DEF-audit's qualifier leaves out a class of records that really exists. The branch's premises still do not say whether asserted records, or any other class, rest on an artifact or stamp. Either fix closes the gap: (a) state that only measured or imported records rest on artifacts or stamps, or (b) narrow the claim's first sentence to measured or imported records. Wording only, not part of the gap: the claim's 'reported as information' adds a severity label that AXM does not use (AXM says 'still reported ... does not block'). DEF-set-aside defines 'set aside' for trial records, but defines 'counts' for any record.

reasoning: Attacks tried, each holding every premise: (a) Shared stamp S. Trial T1 recorded digest d1 and is superseded (set aside). Trial T2 recorded d2 = S's current digest and counts. S 'no longer matches the digest a trial resting on it recorded' (T1's), so by DEF-audit S can no longer be audited and gets a finding. By AXM that finding blocks while T2 counts. The claim says the same thing (it blocks while a record resting on S counts), so the claim holds; this is over-blocking relative to the branch's intent, not a failure of the claim. (b) A record that is neither measured nor imported rests on a damaged artifact A and counts, while the measured record on A is set aside. AXM blocks on 'any record' and the claim blocks on 'a record', so both block. Holds. (c) An artifact or stamp whose record never stored a hash or digest is then altered. By DEF-audit it is not 'no longer auditable' (only a missing artifact qualifies), so there is no finding. The claim's first sentence covers only what can no longer be audited in that defined sense, so it holds vacuously. (d) Transitive resting: record -> stamp -> artifact. The claim and DEF-audit use 'rests on' in the same sense, so whatever reach the audit has, the claim has. (e) Timing: a record counts, then is amended to quarantined. 'Blocks while' is a state predicate taken from AXM, so the finding stops blocking and stays reported. Holds. I could not build any scenario where every premise holds and the claim fails.

Sentence 1 is DEF-audit restricted to the defined term: 'makes a finding for each it can no longer audit' over 'every artifact and every stamp that a measured or imported record rests on, whether or not that record counts'. The claim drops the 'whether or not' clause but keeps 'every', so nothing is narrowed. Sentence 2 instantiates AXM for the findings in sentence 1. Each is 'a finding that a record's artifact or stamp can no longer be audited', so AXM's antecedent is met, and its consequents (blocks while any resting record counts; once none does, still reported with why those records were set aside, does not block) are copied word for word. 'A record ... counts' and 'any record ... counts' are the same existential. Leaving out 'No such finding is dropped' only weakens the claim. Assumptions I checked for: (i) that every record resting on an artifact or stamp is a trial record, so that DEF-set-aside gives 'counts' and 'set aside' their meaning. The claim does not need this, because it uses 'counts' and 'set aside' exactly as AXM does and inherits AXM's presupposition that a record which does not count was set aside. DEF-set-aside grounds the terms for trial records but is not needed for the inference. (ii) That 'can no longer be audited' in AXM is DEF-audit's defined term. It is the same phrase, and DEF-audit defines it with 'exactly when'. No unstated premise is needed.

NOT(claim) needs at least one of these. (1) Some no-longer-auditable artifact or stamp that a measured or imported record rests on gets no finding: contradicted by DEF-audit ('makes a finding for each'). (2) Some such finding does not block while a resting record counts: contradicted by AXM. (3) Once none counts, the finding is unreported, blocks, or carries no reason for the set-aside: contradicted by AXM. (4) The presupposition fails, i.e. a resting record does not count yet was not set aside. For trial records DEF-set-aside rules this out (counts iff not set aside). For any non-trial record no premise makes a record that does not count also not set aside, so this is underivable, not derivable. No premise defines 'counts' in a way that conflicts with AXM's use of it. Nothing in the premises derives the negation.

subject: BRN-audit-blocks-what-counts
text:
These are design and wording observations from the verification pass. They are not gaps; the claim follows from its premises as written.
(1) Over-blocking on a shared stamp. In DEF-audit, a stamp is un-auditable when it no longer matches the digest recorded by *a* trial resting on it, which is existential over trials. Blocking (AXM) is decided per stamp, over *any* counting record. So a superseded trial holding an old digest makes the stamp un-auditable, and the finding then blocks for as long as a fresh, matching, counting trial rests on the same stamp. That is damage that touches only set-aside records but still blocks, which goes against the branch's name. If stamps are never shared across digests this cannot happen, but no premise says so.
(2) Record kinds. DEF-set-aside defines counts and set-aside only for *trial* records. DEF-audit and AXM speak of 'measured or imported' records and of 'a record'. The bridge 'every record that rests on an artifact or stamp is a trial record' is never stated. The claim does not need it, because it inherits AXM's usage, but DEF-set-aside grounds the terms only under that bridge.
(3) A definition oddity. If an artifact or stamp never had a hash or digest recorded, it can only be 'no longer auditable' by going missing. Altering it in place produces no finding, even though in plain language it cannot be audited.
(4) Minor attachment ambiguity. In 'every artifact or stamp a measured or imported record rests on that can no longer be audited', the clause 'that can no longer be audited' could grammatically attach to 'record'. The intended reading, artifact or stamp, is the natural one.

counterexample: The head is commit C, and the snapshot resolves it to C and names it. In the ledger, BRN-x (an id not declared at C) was proposed with statement S1 citing DEF-a. It was then proposed again with statement S2 citing DEF-a and LEM-b and has not been withdrawn, so by DEF-premise-graph its one staged proposal is S2 and S1 is no longer staged. A second id, BRN-y, was proposed and later withdrawn. The snapshot builds the premise graph from C's declarations and the proposals staged in the ledger as it read it: BRN-x is admitted as S2 and BRN-y is absent. For each lemma and branch in that graph it shows the proof state DEF-proof-state gives that node in that build, and no other proof state. For BRN-x that is the state computed from S2 and its current trials. Next to BRN-x's proof state it shows BRN-x's statement as first proposed, S1. In a list of retired proposals it shows BRN-y with its statement and no state. Every premise holds. Each declaration it shows comes from C. The build's sources, the proof states, the issues and gaps, 'shows no state for a contract', 'reads no evidence record', no ledger append, no declaration change and the one page all hold as DEF-snapshot requires. DEF-snapshot says nothing about which proposals the report shows. DEF-ledger, DEF-premise-graph, DEF-proof-state, DEF-current-trial, DEF-belief-eligible and both axioms are untouched. The claim fails: S1 and BRN-y are proposals the snapshot shows, and neither is staged in the ledger as the snapshot read it. A reader also sees S1 beside a proof state computed for S2.
reasoning: The clause 'every proposal it shows is one staged in the ledger as the snapshot read it' has no counterpart in DEF-snapshot. DEF-snapshot bounds the declarations it shows ('takes every declaration it shows from that commit'), the sources of the build, the proof states it shows ('and no other'), the issues and gaps it lists, contract state, evidence records, the ledger and its one page. It never bounds which proposals it shows. A proposal is not a declaration: DEF-premise-graph keeps ids declared at the head revision apart from proposals staged in the ledger. So a snapshot can show a proposal that is not staged and still meet every premise. The scenario below does that. Attacks that failed on the other clauses: (1) Named revision vs head revision. If HEAD moves after the snapshot resolves it to C, the build comes from C and the proof states are 'the proof state DEF-proof-state gives that node in that build'. 'In that build' also carries DEF-current-trial's 'the premise graph' and 'now' to that build. The claim only says the shown state is the one in the graph built from the named revision, not the node's state at the new head, so nothing in it breaks when the two come apart. (2) The page changing a proof state. AXM-commit-is-approval computes every proof state from committed content and the ledger 'and from no other file in the working tree'. The page's directory holds no declaration file and no part of the ledger, so the page is neither. Even committed later by someone else, it would not be a declaration, and DEF-proof-state reads only graph place, the admitted version and trials. (3) The page changing a measured belief. The page is not a trial record and lies outside the ledger, so it is not belief-eligible evidence (DEF-belief-eligible, DEF-ledger). The ledger is append-only and the snapshot appends nothing, so AXM-no-belief-write-path holds belief fixed. Strongest version tried: the snapshot commits its page into a directory nested inside a component's declared code path, which staleness could then act on. DEF-snapshot allows the nesting, because a declaration naming the parent names neither that directory nor anything in it. The commit itself is excluded by 'Besides the report it returns, it writes one page', since a commit would be a further write.

counterexample: Missing premise for clause 2: DEF-snapshot needs a statement, parallel to the one it makes for declarations, that every proposal a snapshot shows (its statement and the premises it cites) is the proposal staged for that id in the ledger as the snapshot read it, i.e. the version its build drew on. Equivalently: a snapshot shows a proposal only as a node of the graph it built. Without it, a snapshot may show a superseded or withdrawn proposal and still satisfy DEF-snapshot. Secondary wording: 'the premise graph built from them' should name its sources (the named revision's declarations and the proposals staged in the ledger as the snapshot read it). DEF-snapshot does not say the snapshot shows every declaration of that commit or every staged proposal, so 'them' read as 'what it shows' would need that premise as well.
reasoning: Clause 1 (declarations as committed at the named revision) follows directly from 'takes every declaration it shows from that commit and from no other version of it, and names that commit'. Clause 3 (the shown proof state is the node's state in the build) follows from 'for each lemma and branch in that graph it shows the proof state DEF-proof-state gives that node in that build, and no other'. That holds when 'them' in 'the premise graph built from them' is read as the named revision's declarations and the staged proposals as read. Read as 'the declarations and proposals it shows', it would also need the snapshot to show every declaration of that commit and every staged proposal, which DEF-snapshot does not state. The second sentence follows. No ledger append and no declaration change mean no proposal is staged, restated or withdrawn, so the graph, the admitted versions, the trials and their currency (DEF-current-trial) are unchanged. AXM-commit-is-approval excludes the uncommitted page from every proof state. AXM-no-belief-write-path, with DEF-belief-eligible and DEF-ledger, excludes a belief change when no trial record is appended. That last step reads 'changes only through belief-eligible evidence' as 'only by belief-eligible evidence recorded in the ledger'. I accept that as the axiom's plain sense. Clause 2 is the step with no premise behind it. The derivation rule states only where the graph's proposals come from, never which proposals the snapshot shows, and then asserts the latter.

For clause 1, clause 3 and the second sentence, NOT(claim) cannot be derived. Each follows from a DEF-snapshot clause together with AXM-commit-is-approval, AXM-no-belief-write-path, DEF-belief-eligible, DEF-ledger, DEF-premise-graph, DEF-proof-state and DEF-current-trial, and no premise supports a snapshot that shows an off-commit declaration, shows a proof state from another build, or moves a belief or proof state. Clause 2 is evenly balanced. The premises do not entail that every shown proposal is staged, and they do not entail that some shown proposal is not. The claim follows if one adds 'a snapshot shows a proposal only as a node of its build'. Its negation follows just as easily if one adds 'a snapshot also lists the proposal history', and nothing in DEF-snapshot prefers one addition to the other. On clause 2 the premises are too weak to decide the claim either way.

subject: DEF-snapshot
text: Noticed while verifying BRN-snapshot-shows-one-revision; this carries no proof weight. (1) The rule on where the page goes ('a directory of the working tree that holds no declaration file and no part of the ledger and that no declaration names; where a declaration names that directory or anything in it, it writes nothing') does not keep the page out of a component's declared code path. Suppose a component declares a parent path P and the page directory is P/sub. The declaration names neither P/sub nor anything inside it, so the page may land inside the component's code. Taking the snapshot still changes no belief, because the page stays uncommitted and AXM-commit-is-approval and AXM-no-belief-write-path cover that. But the next commit that sweeps in the working tree would change that component's code at head, and that could stale evidence that names an older commit. If the author wants to exclude this, the condition could also say that no declaration names the directory, anything in it, or anything that contains it. (2) DEF-snapshot says 'names that commit' but not that it names no other revision, and BRN-snapshot-shows-one-revision relies on 'the one revision it names'. That is a minor presupposition; it is not a gap I could turn into a trial. (3) The only place DEF-snapshot says a write is bounded is 'Besides the report it returns, it writes one page'. Excluding a commit by the snapshot, and therefore a head move, depends on reading that sentence as exhaustive. Saying outright that it creates no commit and moves no ref would remove the dependence.

reasoning: Attacks tried, each with every premise held. (1) Head moves between resolution and reading: a commit lands after the snapshot resolves head to C1, so head is C2 when declarations are read. DEF-snapshot takes every declaration it shows from the resolved commit and from no other version, and builds from that commit's declarations, so what it shows is as committed at C1, the one revision it names; the claim names 'that revision', not head, so it holds. (2) Uncommitted edits: a declaration file's working copy differs from C1. DEF-snapshot names the file as carrying uncommitted edits and does not show them, so no shown declaration departs from C1. (3) A proposal restated mid-read: the claim's proposal and build clauses are pinned to 'the ledger as the snapshot read it', exactly as DEF-snapshot pins them, so no reading of that phrase satisfies the premise and breaks the claim. (4) Proof state shown versus build: DEF-premise-graph's admission rule gives a unique admitted set (the nodes whose citation closure is acyclic and fully present), whatever order nodes are admitted in, so 'the proof state that node has in that build' is determinate; DEF-snapshot shows exactly the state DEF-proof-state gives in that build, and no other. (5) Proof state moved through the two written files: the page and the ignore file sit in a directory holding no declaration and no part of the ledger. By AXM-commit-is-approval a proof state is computed from committed content and the ledger and from no other working-tree file, and the snapshot makes no commit, does not move head and writes nothing else, so neither input changes. Even an ignore file that overwrites a tracked file in that directory changes only the working tree. (6) Proof state moved through currency: no trial or amendment is appended, and the graph and every admitted version are unchanged, so by DEF-current-trial the fingerprints, validity and membership in the graph of every trial are unchanged. (7) Strongest attack, measured belief moved through a written file: a declared test reads the snapshot's page through a glob without naming it on its run line or among what it reads, so DEF-snapshot's guard does not stop the write. A later run of that test then measures a different outcome, its trial is recorded and the posterior moves. This does not falsify the claim. The belief moves at the later run, through measured evidence that AXM-no-belief-write-path admits; taking the snapshot itself appends no record and changes no declaration in effect, so no belief differs between before and after the snapshot. Recorded as a note, not a counterexample.

Clause by clause. Declarations shown: the claim's 'as committed at the one revision it names' is DEF-snapshot's 'names that commit and no other revision, and takes every declaration it shows from that commit and from no other version of it', and it is no wider. Proposals shown: worded identically to DEF-snapshot. Proof states shown: the claim's build ('that revision's declarations and the proposals staged in the ledger as the snapshot read it') is DEF-snapshot's build, and 'the one that node has in that build' is DEF-snapshot's 'the proof state DEF-proof-state gives that node in that build'. The time at which trials are read is left open in both alike, so the claim is not wider there either. No measured belief moves: AXM-no-belief-write-path allows a change only through belief-eligible evidence under the declarations in effect. DEF-belief-eligible makes such evidence a trial record that a server ran or imported and recorded, which DEF-ledger counts among the trials the servers keep. The snapshot appends no record, changes no declaration and makes no commit, so it adds no evidence and leaves the declarations in effect unchanged (AXM-commit-is-approval). A working-tree write cannot reach a belief except through evidence, by the same axiom; the guards for component code and declared tests close that route further, though the derivation does not need them. No proof state moves: the graph inputs (declarations at head and staged proposals) are unchanged because the snapshot does not commit, does not move head and appends nothing to an append-only ledger, which together exclude staging, restating or withdrawing any proposal. The admitted versions, the trials on each node and their currency (DEF-current-trial) are therefore unchanged. The written files fall outside every proof-state input by AXM-commit-is-approval and by DEF-snapshot's 'writes two files and nothing else'. The one inferential step not spelled out is that belief-eligible evidence has to be appended to the ledger, or committed, to take effect. It follows from DEF-belief-eligible ('recorded against a contract'), DEF-ledger and AXM-commit-is-approval together, so it is not a gap.

To derive NOT(claim), the premises would have to allow a shown declaration from another revision, a shown proposal or proof state from another build, or a ledger, commit, head or declaration effect. DEF-snapshot rules out each of these explicitly, and AXM-commit-is-approval rules out a working-tree route to any proof state. Strongest attempt, explosion: DEF-snapshot says the snapshot 'reads no evidence record', yet it must show proof states, which by DEF-proof-state need 'the trials recorded on it'. If 'evidence record' covered the verification trials, DEF-snapshot would be unsatisfiable for any node with trials, and both the claim and its negation would follow vacuously. No premise defines 'evidence record'. In DEF-snapshot it is paired with 'shows no state for a contract', and DEF-belief-eligible uses 'evidence' for trial records made against a contract. The consistent reading, evidence recorded against contracts, is therefore the natural one, and under it the premises do not support the negation. The ambiguity is recorded separately as a note for the author.

subject: BRN-snapshot-shows-one-revision
text: Verifier observations that are not trials (from the 2026-10-06 pass on the 745b545 statement). (a) DEF-snapshot's 'reads no evidence record' is undefined. If it is read as covering the verification trials that DEF-proof-state needs in order to compute a proof state, DEF-snapshot contradicts its own clause that the snapshot shows those proof states. Stating it as, for example, 'reads no record made against a contract' would remove the ambiguity. (b) DEF-snapshot's write guard applies where a declared test 'names either on its run line or among what it reads'. A test that reads the snapshot's page through a glob or a directory walk without naming it is not covered, so a later run of that test can measure a different outcome because the page exists. The claim survives this, since the belief moves at the later run through measured evidence and not at the snapshot. If the guard is meant to close that channel, it is narrower than its purpose. (c) The claim does not say that a proposal it shows is the version the build admitted for that id, only that both come from 'the ledger as the snapshot read it'. If that phrase allows more than one read of the ledger, a proposal shown beside a proof state could differ from the version the proof state was computed for. The claim and DEF-snapshot share the same phrase, so this is not a gap; it is an open coherence property the author may want to state.

subject: BRN-snapshot-shows-one-revision
text: Correction to point (a) of my earlier note. The tree shows that DEF-evidence-record is declared ('a trial record in the evidence ledger is recorded against exactly one contract'). That definition settles 'reads no evidence record' in the consistent sense: it means contract evidence, not verification trials. Neither DEF-snapshot nor this branch cites it, though, so the reading still depends on the term's name and not on a citation. If DEF-snapshot cited DEF-evidence-record, the term would be tied to that definition by citation.

counterexample: Scenario 1 (staged node restated and restored between revisions). Node N is in the premise graph as a staged proposal with statement S and cited premises P. A code link L is committed at revision r0. Its region R is well formed, carries an id no other region carries, and sits in a scanned tracked file. L points to N; its body pin is R's body digest and its claim pin is N's claim digest at r0. After r0 and before any further commit, N's staged proposal is re-proposed with statement S' (so N is restated under DEF-restatement), then re-proposed with S and P again (restated again). Commit r1 then changes only an unrelated file. At r1, R's code is unchanged, so the body digest equals the body pin. N is in the premise graph with the same statement and premises, so its fingerprint is unchanged (DEF-current-trial). Its dependency set and their fingerprints are unchanged, so its claim digest equals the claim pin (DEF-code-link). By DEF-aligned-link, L is aligned at r1, and by the claim's first sentence it reads aligned at r1. But N 'has been restated since its claim pin was taken', and r1 is the first revision at which that holds, so the claim's second sentence says L stops reading aligned at r1. Every premise holds and the two sentences of the claim contradict each other. Withdrawing N and re-staging an identical proposal before r1 does the same for 'removed'. Scenario 2, independent of the first: a code link is declared in comments of a file git tracks (DEF-code-link) that is not among the scanned files. AXM-links-never-silent covers only links in scanned files, so nothing reports this link at any revision. At a revision where it is aligned it does not read aligned, and after its region's code changes it is not reported 'with why'. Both are contrary to the claim, and both are consistent with every premise.
reasoning: Attack on 'the first revision at which ... its node, or any node its node depends on, has been restated or removed since its claim pin was taken'.
